paragraphs: Rock piles, not a bottle label, decide whether an African cichlid spends the day grazing or pinned in a corner. Malawi mbuna, Tanganyikan reef fish, and Victorian haps share 76 to 82°F, pH 7.8 to 8.6, and a floor of 55 gallons, with general hardness held around 12 to 20 dGH. Mbuna need spirulina and vegetable foods. Peacocks and haps take a broader pellet and frozen mix. Park every new fish in its own cycled tank until it eats and tests read 0 ppm ammonia and 0 ppm nitrite, because a sick mbuna inside a crowded cave stack is miserable to catch.

A cockatoo and a blackwater agassizii can both be sold under one genus name, and both still belong on the soft side of pH 5.0 to 7.0. The printed span of 72 to 86°F is wide because Apistogramma is many species, so match the heater to the fish you actually bought and give it a 20-gallon tank with sand plus a cave. These omnivores do better on tiny meaty foods than on jumbo cichlid sticks. Semi-aggressive, here, is a female on eggs, which is why a second male and very timid tankmates are a bad mix. Hold the newcomer apart until the belly fills and the fins stay spread.

Do not mature a filter with an Apistogramma. These dwarf cichlids come from soft acidic forest water, and ammonia from an unfinished cycle burns gills that never evolved for a new-tank spike. Run the 20-gallon setup until a test kit shows ammonia at 0 ppm, nitrite at 0 ppm, and nitrate present but near the 20 ppm mark, with the heater inside 72 to 86°F. A bottled bacteria product can shorten the wait. It does not replace those readings. Only then should the fish go in.

Mouth size sets the menu for this 2 to 3 inch omnivore. A pellet made for an oscar sinks, sits, and rots in the sand while the Apistogramma never takes a bite. Offer a fine pellet, baby brine shrimp, and frozen daphnia, and stop when the fish lose interest after a minute or two. Leftover protein in a warm, low-flow cave tank is how nitrate climbs and a pair starts looking washed out. Feed on a schedule you can watch, and skip the next offering if uneaten worms are still on the substrate. Three to 5 years is too short a life to spend on a swollen belly or an empty one.

Change the food across the week instead of parking a dwarf cichlid on a single flake tin. A meat-heavy day puts color into a male's fins, and a prepared pellet day fills in what frozen worms leave out. When a fish that used to dart from the cave now stays inside, stop experimenting with new jars and test the water before you call it fussy. A brooding female often ignores food for a short stretch, and that pause looks nothing like a fish clamped under the surface film. Note what was eaten so the next refusal stands out.

Look at the cave mouth during a feed, not at your own reflection in the glass. A settled Apistogramma slips out, takes a worm, and backs into cover. White grains on the dark bars, a fraying tail, or a belly that stays pinched are the changes that count. Ich, fin rot, and bacterial redness show first on a fish whose soft water has drifted. Catch it while it still eats. This card is not a dose chart, so if the animal fades after ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate test where they should, ask a fish veterinarian rather than guessing a remedy.

House each new Apistogramma in a separate cycled tank, near the pH you already run and inside 72 to 86°F, before it meets a female that owns a cave. A couple of weeks of steady appetite is the useful observation window for a semi-aggressive dwarf that will vanish into decor the moment it is scared. Adding a sick fish means pulling the hardscape apart to net it. Do not pour a random remedy into that holding tank on a hunch. If spots or ragged fins appear, keep the display untouched and identify the problem with a veterinarian or a keeper who knows this genus.

A silver arowana eats like the predator it is, and the 250-gallon minimum exists because that appetite belongs to a fish that reaches 24 to 36 inches. Offer meaty foods sized to the mouth: prawn, earthworm, and a quality carnivore pellet, at 75 to 82°F, and take leftovers out before they foul a tank this large. Feeder goldfish are a poor staple. They often carry parasites and teach the arowana to ignore prepared food. One heavy meal that the fish finishes beats three handfuls that rain onto the bottom and spike nitrate past 20 ppm. Ammonia at 0 ppm is marked critical on this card for a reason.

Rotate the carnivore menu so a 15 to 20 year fish does not live on a single frozen item. Prawn one day, a sinking carnivore pellet the next, and an earthworm or two as a treat covers more ground than market shrimp alone. Watch the surface from the side. A healthy arowana tracks food the moment it hits the water and takes it in one upward strike. A fish that lets pellets drift past the barbels is telling you something is off, long before the body looks thin. Stop adding new foods and check ammonia, nitrite, and temperature before you blame the brand.

Surface feeding is the whole hunting style. Osteoglossum and Scleropages look up, surge, and leave the water if the lid is ajar, so feed with the cover nearly closed and your hand clear of the gap. Scatter food along the length of a 250-gallon tank rather than dumping it in one corner, or a semi-aggressive arowana guards that splash and any tankmate underneath never eats. Target a shy fish with tongs if you keep bottom dwellers that must not compete at the surface. Night feeding is a bad habit. These fish are visual hunters, and food they miss becomes waste under the filter intake.

Learn the normal hover. A healthy arowana holds near the surface, eyes tracking, fins relaxed, at 75 to 82°F. Clamped fins, a tilt, white specks along the huge scales, or a refusal to rise for prawn are the deviations that matter on a fish you cannot easily net from 250 gallons. Ich and bacterial fin damage show up late on a dark-backed animal if you only glance while the lights are bright. Spend a minute at feeding and another with the lights dim. If the fish declines after ammonia and nitrite read 0 ppm, involve a veterinarian. Do not invent a bath or a dose for an animal this size.

Quarantine for an arowana means a second large, cycled, lidded tank, not a bucket. A juvenile still grows fast, and anything you add to a 250-gallon display is nearly impossible to remove once it is sick. Keep the new fish at 75 to 82°F, pH between 6.0 and 7.5, and watch it eat meaty foods for several weeks before it meets tankmates it might swallow or infect. Asian arowana, Scleropages formosus, are CITES-listed. Buy only fish you can keep legally, and do not treat paperwork as optional. The quarantine tank is also where you confirm you bought a silver, not a protected species sold under the wrong name.

The satisfying part of an arowana is the decade and a half you get if the lid stays shut and the adult has 250 gallons. Most regrets start with a 6-inch fish in a tank that cannot hold a 3-foot carnivore. Silver arowana from South American floodplains are the animals hobbyists can realistically plan for. A jumping fish on the floor is not a mystery. It is an open gap, a loose cable, or a hood lifted at feeding time. Get the cover, the filter, and the adult footprint right, and the fish becomes the calm surface hunter people hoped to keep.

Budget for the adult, not the juvenile in the shop photo. A fish listed at 24 to 36 inches, expert care, and 250 gallons minimum will need a canister or sump that can handle a carnivore's waste, plus replacement media, meaty food, and electricity for heat at 75 to 82°F across 15 to 20 years. People who price only the purchase later cut water changes, and ammonia on this card is marked critical. A realistic plan includes a second heater or a way to heat that volume if one unit dies, and a lid that will not flex when a startled fish hits it. The cheap setup is the one that fits the adult on day one.

Heater failure in 250 gallons is slow, which makes it easy to miss, and filter failure is fast. A silver arowana at 75 to 82°F in a large volume will not crash in an hour the way a 5-gallon shrimp tank might, but a winter power cut in a cold room still walks the temperature down overnight, and a carnivore that stops eating is hard to restart. Worse is a dead canister on a fish this size: ammonia is listed as critical, and 0 ppm becomes a fantasy by the next morning. Keep a spare heater rated for the volume, a thermometer you actually read, and a way to move water if the filter stops. A battery air pump does not replace a biological filter on a 3-foot predator.

Buy the filter and the lid as if they have to outlast a 15 to 20 year carnivore, because they do. A bargain hood that lifts when an arowana strikes is not a savings on a 250-gallon system you cannot rebuild in an afternoon. Canister seals, impeller parts, and a second heater cost less than cycling a new giant tank after an ammonia spike. The fish, the rock or driftwood you finally got stable, and any tankmates that survived the first year are the investment. Expert care on this card is mostly reliable equipment plus the habit of looking at it.

Years with an arowana are won by the same dull habits: a shut lid, meaty meals that get finished, and water that stays at 0 ppm ammonia inside 75 to 82°F. A prettier light fixture will not fix a fish that has outgrown a tank below the 250-gallon minimum. Track nitrate, watch the surface hover, and replace tired gear before it fails on a holiday. That is the husbandry that still matters in year ten, when the silver is longer than your arm and the room has been arranged around the tank.

Clea helena earns its keep by eating other snails, so the husbandry has to match a hunter, not a glass-cleaner. Give this 0.75 to 1.25 inch snail 10 gallons or more, sand it can burrow in, 72 to 78°F, and pH 7.0 to 8.0 with general hardness around 8 to 15 dGH. Soft acidic water pits the shell. A new assassin should live apart from nerites and mystery snails until you mean to deploy it, because it will take ornamental snails as readily as bladder snails and ramshorns. Measured feeding matters once the pests thin out: a sinking pellet or a bit of meat keeps it from starving in a tank it has already cleaned of prey.

What people enjoy about an assassin snail is the slow detective work, a striped shell half buried, waiting, in a 10-gallon tank that no longer crawls with ramshorns. That only lasts when the water stays hard enough at 72 to 78°F and someone notices the day the pests are gone. Two or three years is the lifespan on the card. A keeper who adds a crowd of assassins to a small outbreak often ends up with hunters and nothing left for them to hunt, including the nerite that was supposed to stay. Stock the hunter for the job you actually have, and the tank stays interesting instead of empty.

Feed the species printed on the bag, not the family name. A lawnmower blenny, Salarias fasciatus, scrapes film algae and starves in a bare 20-gallon reef that was wiped clean the day it arrived. A midas blenny will take prepared foods in the water column. Hold marine blennies at 72 to 82°F, pH 8.1 to 8.4, and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, in a tank sized inside the 20 to 55 gallon span for the adult you bought. Offer nori or an algae-based gel once the rock film thins, and keep portions small enough that leftovers do not push nitrate above 20 ppm. An omnivore-to-herbivore label is a warning that one menu does not fit every blenny.

Swap foods as the rock changes, because a blenny's grazing shifts with what is growing. Early on, a lawnmower may ignore a pellet and live on the film. Later, the same fish picks at coral mucus if you never replace that film with nori, spirulina, or an herbivore preparation. A bicolor blenny that suddenly refuses the clip of seaweed it used to attack is an early health signal, not a mood. Check salinity, temperature, and whether a tankmate has taken the perch in front of its hole. Four to 6 years of scraping rock only happens when the menu follows the species from herbivore toward omnivore, not the other way around by accident.

Blennies feed from a burrow they defend. Watch the hole, not the open water, at feeding time. A lawnmower darts, rasps, and backs in. A midas may swim up for a pellet, which is normal for that species and a poor clue if you apply it to a tailspot blenny that should stay on the rock. Two algae grazers in one 20-gallon tank will fight over a single favorite crevice and the loser stops eating. Feed so both holes get a share, and do not rely on one clip of nori placed on the winner's porch. Appetite at the burrow tells you more about this fish than color does under a blue reef light.

A blenny that stays in the hole through feeding, breathes fast, or shows white specks against the rock is not having a shy day. Marine ich and marine velvet both move quickly in a reef at 72 to 82°F, and a fish already weakened by an empty stomach has less margin. Learn the normal rhythm of your species: lawnmowers graze all day, while some Ecsenius perch and watch. A change in that rhythm, plus frayed fins or a dusty coat, is the moment to move the fish if you can. Do not dose copper into a reef. Copper harms invertebrates, and this page has no dose to offer. A fish-only hospital tank and a veterinarian are the honest next step.

Quarantine a new blenny in marine water that already matches the display: 72 to 82°F, specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, and a hole to sit in. A bare cup stresses a fish that lives in a crevice, so give it rock or PVC and a bit of nori if it is an algae grazer. Several weeks of watching it eat will show ich or velvet before that fish meets corals and shrimp you cannot medicate. Never run copper in the display. If you and a veterinarian use copper at all, it belongs in a fish-only hospital tank, not on the reef. A hungry lawnmower also needs film or seaweed during the wait, or quarantine itself becomes the thing that starves it.

A blenny that gets a mature reef, a real burrow, and the right end of the 20 to 55 gallon range becomes a fish you notice every time you walk past. Lawnmowers work the rock. Midas blennies flash yellow in the open. That engagement depends on salinity staying at 1.020 to 1.025 and on somebody feeding nori after the natural film is gone. Easy care on this card describes common grazers in a tank that already has food on the rocks, not a fang blenny and not a new box of dry live rock. Commit to the species you named, and the perch at the hole stays occupied for the 4 to 6 year lifespan.

Marine costs follow the species you picked inside this family. A small blenny in 20 gallons still needs salt mix, a skimmer or other reef filtration, tests for salinity and nitrate, and algae-based food once the rocks are bare. A fish headed toward 6 inches belongs nearer 55 gallons, and the electricity and salt scale with that box. People who budget only the livestock later skip water changes, and nitrate above 20 ppm shows up as a blenny that hides and a reef that slimes. Plan replacement parts for the heater and return pump before a long weekend, because a reef at 72 to 82°F does not pause while a part is on order.

A heater that sticks on in a 20-gallon reef can shove a blenny out of the 72 to 82°F band in a single afternoon, while the same failure in a 55-gallon tank takes longer and is easier to shrug off. Either way the fish loses its burrow routine, stops grazing, and becomes an easy target for marine ich. A failed return pump is the other half of the problem: oxygen and flow drop, and a bottom dweller in a stale pocket declines while fish at the surface still look fine. Read the thermometer daily. Keep a spare heater sized to the tank you actually run, and a way to move water if the pump dies. Top-off with fresh water only, or a hot tank plus rising salinity hits the blenny from two sides.

Spend money on the heater controller, the lid, and the pump that keeps a blenny's hole oxygenated, not on a brighter light the fish never asked for. Most blennies are reef-safe grazers, and the livestock around them, corals and shrimp included, is what a cheap failed heater destroys. A fish living 4 to 6 years will see at least one pump wear out. Parts on the shelf cost less than a reef crash at a specific gravity you can no longer hold because the return line dumped water on the floor. Match the gear to the tank size inside the 20 to 55 gallon range, and replace it when it sounds wrong rather than when it has already stopped.

Stable saltwater does more for a blenny than any brand of supplement. Hold 72 to 82°F, specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, and pH 8.1 to 8.4, and feed the diet that matches the species, algae for a lawnmower and prepared foods for a midas that actually leaves the rock. Quarantine new arrivals with a burrow and without copper in the display. A blenny that grazes, backs into the same hole, and comes out again tomorrow is the welfare signal. Gadgets do not replace that loop.

Chromis viridis feeds in the open water above coral, so flake that falls straight into the sand never becomes the meal. In a reef of at least 30 gallons, held at 72 to 82°F, pH 8.1 to 8.4, and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, offer a small marine pellet plus frozen mysis or brine shrimp where the school actually swims. These omnivores can take an algae-based flake as part of the rotation, but a thin fish from a wholesale system puts weight on meaty frozen food. Feed a little, twice, and net what they miss so nitrate stays near the 20 ppm ceiling. A single chromis eating in a corner is not a school being fed.

Vary the omnivore menu across the week and watch who reaches it. Mysis one evening, a marine pellet the next morning, and a rinse of brine shrimp later will show you the fish that has stopped competing. A blue green chromis that hangs back and turns olive while the others stay blue-green is an early warning, often hunger, solitude, or nitrate, not a lighting effect. Keep at least a small group, the card's 3 to 5 fish in 30 gallons, so one animal is not picked off the food. If the whole school suddenly ignores a food they rushed yesterday, test salinity and temperature before you open another jar.

On the reef these fish pack above branching coral and pick plankton from the current. Copy that in the tank with open water over rockwork, and feed in that upper band rather than at the substrate where wrasses and hermits win. A school of Chromis viridis should face the same direction and surge together. If one fish is pinned behind the rock during every feed, the group is too tight for the 30-gallon minimum or a newcomer was added late and is being harassed. Peaceful describes a real school with room, not three fish in a cube with no swimming lane. Scatter the food so the rear of the group gets a share.

Color is the daily chart for this species. A healthy blue green chromis shifts between blue and green as it turns. Olive-brown, rapid breathing, white specks, or a dusty gold film means you look closer the same day. Marine ich and marine velvet both spread in water at 72 to 82°F, and a schooling fish that leaves the group is often the first to show it. Compare the loner to the fish still packing over the coral. Do not treat the display with copper if shrimp or corals live there. Move the sick fish to a fish-only hospital tank and get veterinary help. No dose belongs on this page.

Quarantine the school together. A lone Chromis viridis in a bare box often stops eating, which hides the very illness you are trying to see. Match 72 to 82°F and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, give them open water and a coral skeleton or rock to hover over, and feed mysis where they swim. Several weeks of watching the group eat and hold blue-green color is the point of the wait. Ich and velvet show here, before the fish meet a reef you cannot medicate. If copper is used at all, a veterinarian directs it in a fish-only tank. It never goes into the display with invertebrates.

Eight to 15 years is a long contract for a fish that shops sell as a cheap dither. A 30-gallon reef at 72 to 82°F with specific gravity held at 1.020 to 1.025, and a school large enough to rest above the rock, is what makes Chromis viridis worth walking over to see. Replace losses so the last fish is not left alone and fading. The peaceful schooling temperament on the card assumes that group. Commit to salt mix, testing, and a lid, because this species spooks and jumps. Do that, and the blue-green pack over the coral is still there years after the receipt has faded.

A school that can live 8 to 15 years quietly consumes salt, test kits, frozen mysis, and replacement parts for a reef of 30 gallons or more. People who price one fish forget that nitrate control, a protein skimmer where you run one, and electricity for 72 to 82°F continue whether the chromis were inexpensive or not. Cutting water changes to save salt is how color muddies and disease finds a thin fish. Budget the frozen food and the salt mix as repeating purchases, and keep a spare heater before you need it on a weekend when the display is already at the edge of the temperature band.

Small reef tanks punish a stuck heater. In 30 gallons, a failed-on heater can push Chromis viridis above 82°F while evaporation raises salinity if the top-off is neglected at the same time. A failed-off heater in a cool room drops a tropical school out of 72°F overnight, and the fish pack tighter, darken, and stop taking mysis. Either swing is when marine ich shows up. Check the thermometer against a second one. Size a spare heater to this tank, not to a guess, and keep a small pump or air stone ready if the return fails. A schooling fish in stale, hot, salty water declines as a group, which looks dramatic and is usually just equipment.

The equipment that protects a chromis school is boring: a heater that holds 72 to 82°F, a lid or mesh they cannot jump through, and flow that keeps plankton-style food in the water long enough to eat. Corals and invertebrates sharing that 30-gallon reef are worth more than the fish and are the reason a bargain heater is a poor place to save. Pumps and heaters wear out inside an 8 to 15 year lifespan. Buy the replacement while the first unit still runs. A specific gravity of 1.020 to 1.025 is easier to hold with gear that does not dump water on the cabinet.

Blue velvet shrimp graze biofilm and soft algae, and a sterile 5-gallon tank has none of that. Neocaridina davidi of this color line do best at 68 to 74°F, with general hardness about 6 to 8 dGH, carbonate hardness 2 to 5 dKH, and TDS around 150 to 250 ppm. Once the glass is clean, a shrimp pellet or a blanched vegetable replaces the grazing they just finished. Feed sparingly. Leftovers in a small volume push nitrate toward 20 ppm and foul the molt. These are not fish, and a heater set for a betta at 80°F is already above the band where a blue colony breeds and keeps its color.

Rotate grazing foods rather than pouring one flake for the fish and hoping the shrimp find crumbs. A pellet day, a bit of blanched spinach, and a mature patch of biofilm cover more of what this omnivorous scavenger actually uses. Watch a berried female. If she stops picking while the others still work the moss, test temperature and TDS before you add another food. Loss of interest in a usual pellet, especially with a failed molt or a sudden fade from deep blue, is a husbandry signal in a 1 to 2 year animal. One food brand will not carry a colony that lives on variety it used to find growing on the wood.

Feeding is a floor activity. Blue velvets pick, don't chase, and they lose every race to a fast fish hovering at the surface. Drop shrimp food after the lights dim, under Java moss or near cholla, so it reaches the animals the card expects to eat biofilm, algae, and decaying plant matter. A colony that rushes a pellet and then scatters back into the plants is behaving normally. A pile of shrimp stacked on one slice while others hide may mean you are underfeeding, or that the tank is hotter than 74°F and they are stressed into a corner. Count the eyes. If food vanishes and the count drops, something with a mouth is eating shrimp, not just leftovers.

Learn a normal blue velvet day: constant picking, a clear molt on the sand, females with a saddle, and color that stays opaque at 68 to 74°F. The worrying picture is different. Shrimp that stop moving except to twitch, a milky body, a white ring behind the head that never splits, or a colony that was deep blue and turns pale after a water change. Those are the moments to stop dosing anything. Copper, and many fish medicines that contain it, kills Neocaridina. Ich remedies made for fish do not belong here. If the colony crashes, review TDS, temperature, and whether a treatment was used upstream, then ask a keeper who breeds this line or a veterinarian. Do not improvise a cure from a fish bottle.

Quarantine new blue velvets in a cycled shrimp tank, not in a fish hospital that once held copper. Match 68 to 74°F, drip-acclimate, and give them moss and a sponge filter so shrimplets and adults are not sucked into an intake. A few weeks of watching molts tells you whether you imported planaria, scutariella, or a bacterial crash along with the color line. Never medicate this holding tank with a fish remedy on a guess. Keep the colony's own tank free of copper residue from any previous ich treatment. One contaminated net is enough to kill a 5-gallon group that the card lists as beginner and prolific only when the water stays clean.

The purchase price of a blue velvet is the small number. A colony in 5 gallons, or better 10, still needs mineral-stable water at GH 6 to 8 and KH 2 to 5, TDS tests, sponge filters, and food once biofilm runs thin. People underbudget the replacements: a heater that must not overshoot 74°F, a lid, and plants that actually grow. Cutting water changes because the shrimp were cheap is how nitrate passes 20 ppm and a 1 to 2 year colony stalls. Plan on mineral supplements or a remineralized source you can repeat, and on a place for juveniles, because easy breeding on this card will fill the box you bought.

Heater failure for blue velvet shrimp is usually failure in the on direction. They are a cool-water Neocaridina, listed at 68 to 74°F, and many colonies are happier in a stable room than under a heater meant for tetras. A stuck thermostat that climbs toward 80°F stops breeding, fades the blue, and leaves molts half finished. In 5 gallons that climb can happen between breakfast and dinner. If you use a heater at all, size it small and read the thermometer every day. A winter power cut matters less for this species than for a discus, unless the room itself freezes the tank. Filter failure still matters: a dead sponge in a small box lets ammonia rise above 0 ppm, and shrimp die before fish would have looked bothered.

Buy the sponge filter, the thermometer, and the lid before you buy a higher grade of blue. A 1 to 2 year colony that breeds will outgrow a sloppy 5-gallon setup, and the juveniles are the value you are protecting. A strong hang-on-back intake without a cover eats shrimplets. A heater with no backup reading cooks adults that were supposed to stay under 74°F. Dark substrate, moss, and cholla are husbandry here, not decoration, because biofilm on those surfaces is the staple between pellets. Spend on stable water and safe hardware. The color grade cannot survive a copper trace or a hot afternoon that the equipment allowed.

Bolivian rams sift. A pair works the sand with their faces, spits, and picks small animals and leftover bits, which is the feeding behavior worth building a tank around. In 20 gallons or more, offer food they can find on the bottom after that search, not a pile of floating flakes they have to break formation to reach. They are very peaceful dwarfs, so they lose food to pushy tankmates. Feed after the faster fish are done, or target the pair over open sand. If one ram hovers and never sifts while the other eats, you are seeing rank or illness, and the sand-search is the clue. Live or frozen foods tossed across the substrate keep that search going. A single pellet pile under the filter does not.

These are small omnivores, about 3 to 3.5 inches, with a 4 to 7 year lifespan when meals match that size. Use a soft pellet they can chew, plus frozen bloodworm or brine shrimp a few times a week, in portions gone within a couple of minutes. Uneaten protein in a planted 20-gallon tank becomes nitrate, and rams show it as faded color and a refusal to sift. The card's food budget runs about 50 to 150 dollars a year, which is enough for a rotation if you are not buying jumbo cichlid sticks they cannot swallow. Feed young pairs a little more often than settled adults, and skip a day when the sand is still littered. A ram that stays round behind the head is being fed past the point of health.

No single tin covers a Bolivian ram that both sifts for meaty prey and picks at softer foods. Alternate a quality pellet with frozen daphnia or brine so you can see appetite change against a known favorite. A fish that ignores brine but still takes pellet may simply be full. A fish that ignores both, stops sifting, and clamps its fins is an early illness sign in a species listed as beginner partly because it is hardier than its German cousin, not because it is indestructible. Note the food and the response. That log is more useful than another jar when something goes quiet in a very peaceful pair.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress show on Bolivian rams as white grains, ragged edges, redness, or a pair that has stopped sifting and sticks to the heater. Excellent water is the prevention that actually matches this fish. They are very peaceful and do not cope well with constant chasing, which is a stress path into those same problems. Quarantine new fish for a few weeks in a cycled tank before they join the display. Keep a hospital tank ready, but do not stock it with a guesswork remedy or a scooped dose. If spots spread after the water tests clean, ask a veterinarian. Aquarium salt is not a plan by itself, and this card gives no amount to add.

The useful minute is feeding, when a healthy Bolivian ram should be on the sand, face down, chewing. Learn that picture for your pair: color in the face, fins out, both animals eating. A fish that faces the corner, breathes fast, or develops a sunken belly over several days has left that baseline. White spot and frayed fins are easier to see on the lighter body of this species than on a dark cichlid, so use that advantage and look. Catch problems while the ram still takes food. A dwarf that has stopped eating in a decorated tank is difficult to treat, and no dose on a forum replaces a clean test kit and a vet when the decline continues.

Quarantine Bolivian rams as a pair or a small group if they arrived together, in a cycled tank with sand and a cave, before they meet busier fish. They are very peaceful, so a hospital tank with a loud, aggressive dither stresses them into hiding the symptoms you need to see. Several weeks of normal sifting and eating is the observation that earns a move to the 20-gallon or larger display. Do not add medications on a schedule just because the fish is new. If ich appears in quarantine, keep it there, away from the main tank, and get dosing advice from a veterinarian rather than from a bottle chosen at random.

Set the 20-gallon tank up and cycle it before you go looking for Bolivian rams. They want sand they can sift, gentle cover, and tankmates that will not bully a very peaceful dwarf. The card's setup range of about 100 to 500 dollars and a fish price that can run from about 5 to 100 dollars should be spent on that ready tank, not on an animal waiting in a bag. Read keepers who actually run this species beside German blue rams, because the Bolivian fish is the more forgiving of the two and still declines in a fresh, uncycled box. Have the test kit in the drawer the week before the fish comes home.

Build the aquascape like a quiet sandy margin, not like a Malawi rock pile. Bolivian rams sift, so a fine sand bed and a few leaves or smooth stones give them work without shredding their mouths. A cave or a coconut they can hover under supports a pair, and rooted plants will be dug, so attach ferns and Anubias to wood. Moving every decoration each week only destroys the map a peaceful pair has learned. Shift one piece occasionally if a fish is pacing, and leave the feeding sand open. Natural foraging on that sand reduces stress more than a rearrange done for the keeper's eye.

Hunting is the enrichment that fits this ram. Scatter frozen brine or daphnia across the sand and let the pair sift for it, instead of dropping a cube in one frozen lump. Live foods, when you can get them from a clean source, extend that search. Dry pellets still have a place, but they do not replace the face-down feeding that tells you the fish feels safe. A Bolivian ram that no longer hunts a scattered feed, in a tank where it used to, is an early health flag. Use that change. Do not wait for the fish to lie on its side before you test the water and look at the fins.

Buy Bolivian rams from a shop whose tanks are clear, aged, and not crowded with gasping fish, or from a seller who will stand behind a live arrival. Ask to see them eat. A very peaceful dwarf that is already thin in the shop has used up part of a 4 to 7 year lifespan before you get it home. Avoid a tank of rams covered in white spots, no matter the discount. If you order by mail, open the box promptly and acclimate into a cycled quarantine, not straight onto your display sand. The fish price on this card can be modest or steep. Pay for condition either way.

Plan past the fish. The card puts initial setup around 100 to 500 dollars or more, the ram itself anywhere from about 5 to 100 dollars, yearly upkeep around 200 to 500 dollars, and food around 50 to 150 dollars. Those ranges only work if the 20-gallon or larger tank is already cycled and filtered for a pair that sifts and digs. People who buy the fish first later skip water changes, and a very peaceful species still gets ich and fin rot in dirty water. Add a spare heater and filter media to the yearly figure. A 4 to 7 year life is long enough to replace a cheap heater once, and the replacement is cheaper than a second pair of fish.

Rams sit near the substrate, so a heater that fails off on a winter night cools their sand first while the top of the tank still feels lukewarm to your hand. A heater that fails on cooks that same thin layer of water in a 20-gallon tank before you notice the fish have stopped sifting. Bolivian rams are hardier than German blue rams and do not need discus heat, but a sudden swing still knocks a peaceful pair off food and opens the door to ich. Read a thermometer at the sand, not only at the glass. Keep a backup heater and a way to aerate if the filter stops. A battery air pump helps oxygen during an outage. It does not remove ammonia from a tank that has lost its bacteria's flow.

A reliable heater and a filter you can service matter more than a designer light on a beginner ram tank. The animals are inexpensive on the low end of the card's 5 to 100 dollar range and still represent a cycled 20-gallon aquascape you do not want to tear down after an equipment failure. Buy the model with a readable thermostat and spare media, not the unnamed heater that cannot hold a peaceful pair through a cold week. Plants, sand, and the bacteria living in the filter are part of the cost of starting over. Protect them with gear that lasts a slice of the 4 to 7 year lifespan, and replace a noisy pump before it quits on a holiday.

Driftwood is the feeding plan, not an ornament, for Ancistrus. A bristlenose stays 4 to 6 inches, lives 10 to 15 years, and needs a 20-gallon tank at 73 to 81°F and pH 6.5 to 7.5, with wood it can rasp for fiber plus algae wafers and vegetables after the lights go down. These peaceful, nocturnal fish produce more waste than their size suggests, so nitrate can sit higher than a tetra tank. The card allows about 30 ppm, and ammonia and nitrite still belong at 0 ppm. Quarantine a new pleco with a piece of wood in the holding tank, or it starves while you wait to see whether white spots were hiding on a dark body.

Ten to 15 years of bristlenose keeping is a wood pile, a cave, and water that stays inside 73 to 81°F, not a gadget you bought in month one. Males need bristle-friendly cover if you hope to see spawning, and a 20-gallon tank is the minimum for one fish, with more floor space and extra caves if you keep a pair. A filter rated for the waste, serviced before it clogs with wood dust, outperforms a new light fixture. Track nitrate toward that 30 ppm ceiling and keep ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm. The fish that rasps the same log every night is the one whose husbandry is actually working.

Cycle the 20-gallon tank before the bristlenose arrives, and do not buy this pleco to finish the cycle for you. Ancistrus produces a steady load of waste at 73 to 81°F, and an uncycled filter turns that into ammonia above 0 ppm within days. Wait until tests show ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm and plants or water changes can hold nitrate near 30 ppm or below. Put driftwood in from the start so biofilm has somewhere to grow. A fish listed as easy still dies if it is the first animal in a brand-new box with no wood and no mature filter. Patience here is a test kit and a couple of weeks, not a slogan.

Cardinal tetras are a blackwater school, and the husbandry is the water they came from, not a hardy community label. Keep them at 73 to 81°F and pH 4.6 to 6.2, in at least 10 gallons, with ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm and nitrate near 20 ppm or under. They are peaceful omnivores of about 2 inches, living 4 to 5 years when the school is intact and the chemistry stays soft and acidic. A new group should be quarantined together. Splitting them into a bare cup stops them eating, and you learn nothing. Stable parameters plus a measured pinch of fine food beat any brand of conditioner poured in after the fish are already gasping.

Finish the cycle before you even look at a school of cardinals. These tetras show the full neon-and-red stripe only in finished water, and an ammonia spike in a new 10-gallon tank wipes a group that shops still market as beginner. Test until ammonia is 0 ppm, nitrite is 0 ppm, and nitrate has appeared but stays near 20 ppm, at 73 to 81°F and a pH inside 4.6 to 6.2. Do not chase that pH with a powder the same day the fish arrive. Age the water, add leaf litter if you want the blackwater look, and only then acclimate the school. A newly filled tank is not a slightly inconvenient home. It is the wrong home.

Thriving for a cardinal tetra is a tight school, a red stripe that runs the whole body, and soft acidic water that does not swing every time you top off. Surviving is one pale fish in a hard-water community at the edge of 73 to 81°F, hiding while louder tankmates eat the food. Give them at least the 10-gallon minimum, more length if the school is large, and an omnivore flake or micro pellet they can finish. If you will test pH and nitrate and keep the group together, the 4 to 5 year lifespan is realistic. If the tank is a new, uncycled, alkaline box, choose a different fish.

Galaxy rasboras feed like tiny midwater hunters, not like goldfish waiting under a flake shaker. A one-inch celestial pearl danio picks at micro foods among plants, and in a 10-gallon or larger tank the food has to be small enough to fit that mouth. Scatter powdered fry food, baby brine, or a crushed fine pellet across the planting so the whole peaceful group gets some. Dumping a pinch in one spot lets two bold fish eat and the rest fade. Watch who is out at feeding time. A CPD that no longer leaves the moss when brine shrimp hit the water is telling you about health or harassment, even though the species is listed as peaceful. Live and frozen bits, spread out, keep the hunting behavior that dry dust alone eventually dulls.

Portions for a one-inch omnivore are smaller than most keepers think, and the mess lands in a tank that may be only 10 gallons. Feed a fine pellet or crushed flake they can finish in a minute, plus baby brine or microworms a few times a week, and siphon what reaches the substrate. The card budgets about 50 to 150 dollars a year for food, which covers quality micro food if you are not buying large cichlid pellets that rot uneaten. Overfeeding is the usual way nitrate climbs and a 3 to 5 year nano fish loses condition. Underfeeding is the quiet way a shy fish in the back of the school starves while the front rank looks fat. Watch both ends of the group.

One jar of flakes will not carry a galaxy rasbora that lives by picking varied tiny prey off leaves. Rotate a micro pellet, frozen baby brine or daphnia, and an occasional live food from a clean source. Appetite is your early-warning light on a fish only an inch long. If a celestial pearl danio that used to spark across the front ignores a favorite brine feeding, test the water and count the school before you change brands. Refusal is often the first visible illness in a nano fish whose color is already subtle. Write down what they ate. Memory is a poor log for a fish this small.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress are the problems that actually show on a fish this small, usually as flicking, clamped tiny fins, white grains, or a school that has stopped coming out. Water quality is the prevention. A 10-gallon tank swings faster than a big one, so nitrate and leftover food matter. Quarantine new galaxy rasboras as a group for a few weeks. They are peaceful nano fish and they travel better together than alone. Do not keep a bottle of broad medicine as a plan, and do not dose aquarium salt into a small tank on a guess. If the school declines, ask a veterinarian. A one-inch fish has no margin for a wrong treatment.

Use a magnifying look at feeding, because a one-inch CPD does not give you a big canvas. Healthy galaxy rasboras flick through the plants and take micro food in mid-flight. A fish that sits on a leaf, breathes fast, or loses the pearl spots' brightness against the group has left its baseline. White spot and frayed fins are easy to miss on a dark, tiny body unless you look when they come forward to eat. That daily minute is the whole exam. If several fish change on the same day, think water first, then a pathogen, and do not reach for a dose that was printed for a fish ten times their size.

Quarantine celestial pearl danios as a school in a cycled nano tank with plants or moss, not as a single fish in a bare bowl. They are peaceful, an inch long, and they stop eating when they are alone, which hides disease instead of revealing it. Give them a few weeks at stable water, with micro food, before they join the display. A 10-gallon main tank is already small. Adding unobserved fish to it is how ich arrives with no spare tank to move them into. Skip speculative medications. If you see spots in quarantine, leave the display alone and get advice from a veterinarian rather than dosing both boxes.

Have the planted 10-gallon tank cycled and growing a little film before you buy galaxy rasboras. They are beginner nano fish only when the box is already calm, covered, and free of fish that can eat a one-inch animal. Setup on this card runs about 100 to 500 dollars or more, and the fish themselves about 5 to 100 dollars each, so the money belongs in a ready tank. Talk to keepers who run CPDs specifically. They will tell you about jumping lids and about food that has to be crushed. A forum for oscars will not. Test ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate the week before the bag arrives.

Plant the tank the way a one-inch fish uses it: fine leaves, moss, and open pockets rather than a pile of sharp rock. Celestial pearl danios come from small, planted water, and a bare 10-gallon glass box leaves a peaceful school with nowhere to rest. You do not need to rebuild the scape every weekend. A hard rearrange scatters a nano group that had just started coming to the front. Change one clump if a corner has died back, and keep a clear lane where you can see them feed. Shade and cover do more for their behavior than a new ornament in the center of the sand.

Enrichment for a galaxy rasbora is a moving micro food, not a big worm it cannot swallow. Rinse baby brine into the current across the moss and let the school hunt. Frozen daphnia, broken up, does the same job when live food is unavailable. Pellets still feed them, but a fish that only ever eats a static pile loses the pecking behavior you are using as a health check. When the hunt stops, believe it. On a one-inch, 3 to 5 year fish, a missed feeding pattern is often the only early sign you are going to get.

Choose celestial pearl danios from a shop that keeps them in a lidded, planted tank and can show you a group eating micro food. A single inflated price tag does not matter as much as pinched bellies. The card allows roughly 5 to 100 dollars per fish, which means you can overpay for a thin animal or find a fair group. Mail-order fish need a live-arrival promise and a quarantine tank that is already cycled. Open the box quickly, keep them together, and do not pour them into a community that has not been prepared. A peaceful nano fish arrives healthy or it does not arrive useful at all.

Read the card's ranges before you decide this is a cheap nano project. Setup can run 100 to 500 dollars or more, each fish about 5 to 100 dollars, yearly upkeep about 200 to 500 dollars, and food about 50 to 150 dollars. A 10-gallon tank still needs a lid, a gentle filter, tests, and micro food for a 3 to 5 year school. People who buy the fish and skip the lid lose them to the floor. People who skip water changes lose them to nitrate in a small volume. Put a spare heater or a plan for a cool room into the yearly number. The fish are small. The time they live is not a single weekend.

A 10-gallon tank has almost no thermal mass. If the heater sticks on, a celestial pearl danio school can leave a comfortable range before the evening, and if it fails off in a cold room the same box chills just as fast. These are peaceful nano fish. They respond to that swing by hiding, clamping, and catching ich or a bacterial problem that a stable tank would have shrugged off. Put the thermometer where you see it without moving the lid they like to jump through. Keep a spare heater appropriate to 10 gallons, not a powerful unit borrowed from a 75-gallon tank. If the filter stops, ammonia rises quickly in this volume. An air stone during an outage is a bridge. It is not a cycled filter.

Spend on a lid, a small reliable heater, and a filter gentle enough for a one-inch fish, then stop. The card's livestock can be inexpensive, and the costly part is a planted 10-gallon system you would have to restart, along with any shrimp or other nano animals sharing it. A bargain heater without a decent thermostat is how a tiny school gets cooked. A strong filter intake without a sponge is how they get exhausted. Gear that holds a stable box for the 3 to 5 year lifespan is the purchase that matches the animal. Replace a tired pump while the galaxy rasboras are still eating, not after the tank has clouded.

Cherry barbs stay red when the water is stable and the school is large enough to spread the squabbling. Puntius titteya wants 73 to 81°F, pH 6.0 to 7.5, and at least 20 gallons for a group of six or more, ideally eight to ten, with plants and shade like the slow Sri Lankan streams they come from. They are peaceful omnivores about 2 inches long. Feed a modest pellet or flake they finish, and quarantine new fish as a group so you are not adding ich to a school that is hard to catch in dense crypts. A product name will not fix a tank that is too bright, too bare, or short one male-heavy group. One male to two females keeps the color display from turning into constant chasing.

Decide on cherry barbs by looking at a real school, not by collecting another red fish for a 10-gallon community. You need 20 gallons, shade, and the willingness to keep six or more so males color up instead of harassing a single female. Captive-bred fish matter here. The species is vulnerable in the wild in southwestern Sri Lanka, and a wild-caught bargain is the wrong conservation choice. Talk to keepers who have kept a group through the 4 to 6 year lifespan, and ask what happened when the ratio slipped toward too many males. That conversation will tell you more than a label that only says peaceful.

A good cherry barb tank is a shaded 20-gallon planting where the males are genuinely red and nobody is pinned in the corner. That picture takes 73 to 81°F, a school, and live plants such as crypts, Java fern, or Anubias, plus floating cover. It is a satisfying fish when those pieces are in place, and a pale, fin-nipped fish when they are not. Two to 6 years on the card is long enough to see a group mature if you buy captive-bred animals and keep the nitrite at 0 ppm. Get the school size right at the start. Adding one female later rarely repairs a group that was already lopsided.

Chili rasboras are a 0.7-inch peaceful nano fish, and the welfare work is a small stable tank plus food they can actually swallow. The card starts them at 5 gallons, with a beginner-to-intermediate rating that reflects how little water stands between them and a mistake. Keep ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm, feed a measured dusting of micro food, and quarantine new fish as a school. A single chili in a cup stops swimming and teaches you nothing. They are not a fish you stabilize with a gadget. They are a fish you stabilize by leaving the chemistry alone once it is right and by not adding a hungry centerpiece that can eat them.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress show up on chili rasboras as flicking, a school glued to the surface, tiny frayed fins, or white grains you will miss unless the fish come forward. In 5 gallons those problems follow leftover food and a swing in a very small volume. Quarantine a new group for a few weeks in a cycled nano tank before they join the display. Do not park aquarium salt and a broad medicine in the plan as if a dose existed on this card. It does not. If the school crashes, talk to a veterinarian. A fish this small is easy to overdose with any remedy meant for a goldfish.

Prepare the 5-gallon or larger tank, lid and all, before you order chili rasboras. They are peaceful nano fish with a 4 to 8 year lifespan, which is a long time in a box that can be knocked out of balance by one heavy feeding. Setup costs on the card run about 100 to 500 dollars or more, and the fish about 5 to 100 dollars each. Spend that on a cycled, planted tank and a test kit. Keepers who specialize in Boraras will talk about gentle flow and about food ground smaller than flake. A general aquarium forum will tell you they are just small tetras. They are not.

Think of a dark, planted puddle rather than a rock garden. Chili rasboras use fine leaves and floating shade, and a bare bright 5-gallon tank leaves a peaceful school with nowhere to stand. You do not need to rearrange the hardscape on a schedule. Moving the moss every few days resets a group that had just started to show its red. Tuck one new stem in if a corner is empty, and keep an open inch of water where you can see them. The habitat that calms them is stable cover, not novelty.

Scatter baby brine or a crushed micro pellet through the plants and let a chili school pick it out of the water column. That hunt is the enrichment, and it is also how you see who is missing. A 0.7-inch fish cannot chase a large bloodworm, so live and frozen foods have to be tiny or they become pollution. When the picking stops, test the water the same day. On this species a change in feeding behavior is the early health signal, well before a body this small looks obviously sick.

Buy chili rasboras from a shop that keeps them in a lidded planted tank and will show the group eating, or from a mail seller with a live-arrival guarantee and reviews you can check. The card's range of about 5 to 100 dollars per fish is wide enough to hide a poor animal at either end. Refuse a tank of chilies that are clamped or covered in spots. Acclimate the school into quarantine together. A peaceful nano fish that arrives thin has already spent part of a 4 to 8 year life in somebody else's uncycled water.

Thriving green chromis are a school that stays blue-green in open water, not one fish hiding behind a powerhead. Chromis in a saltwater tank need 72 to 82°F, pH 8.1 to 8.4, specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, nitrate near 10 ppm, and at least 30 gallons so a peaceful group can swim. They are omnivores. A marine pellet and frozen mysis, fed where the school hovers, beat a jar of nori meant for a tang. If you will test salinity, keep a lid on a jumpy fish, and replace schoolmates so the last animal is not alone, an 8 to 15 year lifespan is realistic. A single chromis in a new, unstable reef is only surviving, and often not for long.

A cleaner shrimp's welfare is stable reef water and a molt that completes, not a brand of additive. Keep this 2 to 3 inch invert at 72 to 82°F, pH 8.1 to 8.4, specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, and nitrate near 10 ppm, in at least 10 gallons with a protein skimmer or other real biological filtration. They are peaceful omnivores. Feed them a few times a week, or let them pick leftovers, and do not assume fish will line up to be cleaned. Quarantine new shrimp without copper. Many fish medicines kill them, and a molting animal in a tank that recently held ich treatment can die on a residue. Measured feeding plus a hiding place during the molt matters more than any label on a bottle of reef trace.

Clown loaches are a social bottom fish that gets big, and the three things that matter are a cycled 75-gallon or larger tank, food that reaches the substrate, and new animals quarantined before they join the shoal. Adults pass 12 inches and can live 15 to 25 years. They are peaceful with other fish and rough on each other if you keep one or two instead of a real group. Water has to stay at 0 ppm ammonia and 0 ppm nitrite, because a scaleless loach shows burns and ich quickly when a tank is unstable. Feed sinking foods they can find at dusk. A gadget on the glass does not replace a shoal, a cave, and a filter sized for fish that will keep growing.

Ich is the classic problem on clown loaches, alongside fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress from being kept alone. White spot shows fast on a fish that is scaleless and easily chilled or crowded in a tank under 75 gallons. Prevention is clean, stable water and a group large enough that nobody is pinned and stressed. Quarantine every new loach for a few weeks. They are famous for carrying ich into a display and then being miserable to catch among the driftwood. Do not dose aquarium salt or a broad medicine from memory. This card has no amount, and a scaleless fish is easy to harm. If spots appear, isolate the animal and ask a veterinarian.

Build the 75-gallon tank, the caves, and the filter before you buy a clown loach. A juvenile looks like a small community fish and becomes a foot-long shoaling animal with a 15 to 25 year life. Setup on the card runs about 100 to 500 dollars or more, which may not even reach a proper adult tank, so read that range as a starting hint and plan for the fish's adult size. Talk to keepers who have held a group past the cute stage. They will talk about ich, about clicking at night, and about tanks that had to be upgraded. Buy the larger footprint first if you can.

Give clown loaches a long cave and open sand, like a slow river with wood, not a pile of sharp lace rock they will slice themselves on when they bolt. They are peaceful and social, and they stack in a tube together. Rearranging the entire aquascape every week destroys that shelter and stresses a fish already prone to ich. Add a cave if the group has grown, and leave the old one in place. Plants are secondary. The habitat that matters is smooth cover and floor space in 75 gallons or more.

Clown loaches hunt snails and worms. Drop a sinking pellet, then offer bloodworm or an earthworm at dusk so the shoal can search the sand. That search is the enrichment, and it is how you count heads on a nocturnal fish. Live and frozen foods should come from a clean source. A loach that leaves the cave but will not join a worm feeding has left its baseline. Use that moment to test the water and look for white spot, while the fish is still active enough to see.

Buy clown loaches from a shop that keeps them in a group, in a tank large enough that they are not gasping, or from a seller who guarantees live arrival and has reviews you can read. A single cheap juvenile is how people end up with a lonely 12-inch fish. The card's fish price runs about 5 to 100 dollars, so condition matters more than the low end of that range. Refuse animals with spots or clamped fins. Quarantine the group you intend to keep. Adding one loach later, to a shoal that has already bonded, is harder than buying enough at the start.

A clown pleco is a small wood-eating loricariid, and the husbandry is wood, a finished cycle, and a careful new arrival. Adults stay about 3 to 4 inches, live 10 to 12 years, and need 20 gallons at 73 to 82°F and pH 6.8 to 7.6. The diet is herbivore with wood as the staple, backed by algae sheets, spirulina flakes, blanched vegetables, and algae pellets after lights-out. They are peaceful and they hide, so a new fish should be quarantined with its own piece of wood or it will not eat while you watch for illness. Ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm matter more than the brand of wafer. Nitrate belongs near 20 ppm or below in a tank this size.

Cycle the 20-gallon tank to completion before a clown pleco goes in. People buy this fish as a tiny cleaner and drop it into a new box, where there is no biofilm on wood and the filter is not ready. Wait for ammonia at 0 ppm, nitrite at 0 ppm, and nitrate that you can hold near 20 ppm with water changes, at 73 to 82°F. Put the driftwood in early so it starts to soften and grow film. An uncycled tank plus a wood-eater with nothing to rasp is a predictable loss, even though the card says beginner. The fish is easy only after the wood and the bacteria are already there.

Cycle a tank that can hold the adult, not the juvenile in the shop. A common pleco reaches 15 to 24 inches, and the minimum here is 125 gallons at 72 to 86°F and pH 6.5 to 7.5. An uncycled filter under that animal becomes ammonia above 0 ppm in a hurry, because the waste matches the body. Test until ammonia and nitrite are 0 ppm and nitrate can be kept near 20 ppm with real water changes. Do not add this fish to finish a cycle or to clean a new 20-gallon tank. That story is how common plecos die or get dumped. The card lists beginner care for the water, not for the adult footprint.

An adult common pleco is an omnivore with a large mouth, not an algae vacuum you can forget. Feed algae wafers, vegetables, and a protein item such as a sinking pellet or frozen food, in amounts eaten overnight at 72 to 86°F. Leftovers under a 15 to 24 inch fish will push nitrate past 20 ppm no matter how often you wipe the glass. Daytime hiding is normal. A fish that will not come out for food you know it likes, or that looks sunken despite heavy feedings, needs a water test before a new food. Ten to 15 years of this species is mostly waste management and a varied sinking diet in 125 gallons.

Talk to someone who still has the common pleco they bought as a three-inch cleaner. Ask what tank it lives in now. If the answer is under 125 gallons, you are hearing the problem, not a recommendation. This is a peaceful fish that becomes a roommate the size of a forearm, with a 10 to 15 year lifespan and an omnivore's appetite. People who have done it well will talk about oversized filtration and vegetables, not about a sparkling 10-gallon glass. That conversation is the decision. A care sheet that stops at the juvenile photo is how the fish ends up without a home.

The satisfying version of a common pleco is a large, calm fish rasping wood and vegetables in 125 gallons, at 72 to 86°F, with nitrate under control. The unsatisfying version is a stunted animal in a tank bought for the baby. Peaceful temperament does not shrink the adult. If you have the floor space, the filter, and the habit of water changes, a 10 to 15 year pleco is a remarkable fish to keep. If you wanted an algae crew for a community tank, choose a species whose adult size is measured in inches you can actually house.

Congo tetras need length, a school, and water that does not swing, more than they need a special food tin. Adults reach about 3 to 3.5 inches, live 3 to 5 years, and the card starts them at 30 gallons with a peaceful schooling temperament. Keep ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm. Feed an omnivore flake or small pellet they can take in midwater, and quarantine new fish as a group so the school you add is already eating. A single Congo tetra in a holding cup fades and hides the illness you were trying to spot. Brand-name additives do less than a stable 30-gallon tank with open swimming room above the plants.

Three to 5 years of Congo tetras comes from the school and the water, not from the light you liked in the shop. A 30-gallon or longer tank lets males show flowing fins without the group being cramped into a cube. Keep up the water changes so ammonia and nitrite stay at 0 ppm, and replace tired filter media before the flow dies on a fish that lives in the current. Gear is support. The husbandry is a group large enough to school and a keeper who notices when one fish drops out of it. That habit still matters in year four, when the fins are at their best and a dirty tank would melt them.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress cut the flowing fins that make this species worth keeping. A Congo tetra with ragged edges, white grains, or a clamped profile has usually been chilled, crowded, or dropped into a tank with nitrite. Hold the 30-gallon school in clean water and do not add new fish straight from the shop. A few weeks of quarantine for the group is the practical prevention. Do not stage aquarium salt and a broad medicine as if this card listed a dose. It does not. Long fins are also easy to burn with the wrong treatment. Ask a veterinarian if the school declines after the tests read clean.

Have the 30-gallon tank swimming-length and cycled before you look for Congo tetras. They are beginner-to-intermediate because the school needs space and steady water, not because a juvenile looks easy in a bare sale tank. Setup costs on the card sit around 100 to 500 dollars or more, and each fish around 5 to 100 dollars. Talk to keepers who have kept males through a full fin growth. They will mention open water, subdued light, and groups, not a centerpiece rock. Buy the footprint that lets a peaceful school actually school.

Leave a long open lane above the plants. Congo tetras are midwater schoolers, and a 30-gallon tank packed with ornaments from glass to glass gives them nothing to do but hide. You can change a plant clump if it dies. Do not reshuffle the whole layout every week or the group spends its time relearning the map instead of swimming. Dimmer light and a dark substrate show the fins better and match the quieter water these fish like. The habitat is a lane, not a pile of novelty.

Feed Congo tetras in the open water, a small pellet or frozen brine scattered so the school has to move and sort. That search is the enrichment, and it shows you whether a thin fish is being pushed off the food. Live or frozen foods help, in pieces a 3-inch tetra can take without dragging them to the bottom. If the school stops rising for a food it usually chases, test the water before you buy a different brand. Appetite in the lane is the early health check on a peaceful fish whose fins hide a lot of damage until it is serious.

Purchase Congo tetras from a shop that keeps a real school in clean water, with males showing intact fins, or from a mail seller with a live-arrival guarantee. The card's price of about 5 to 100 dollars per fish tracks size and condition. Walk away from ragged fins and white spots. Acclimate the group into quarantine together so a peaceful schooler is not isolated. A single stunning male with no group behind him is a decoration, not a purchase plan, for a fish that needs the school to thrive.

Ask a keeper what happened when their convicts spawned, not whether the juveniles looked cute. Amatitlania nigrofasciata is an easy omnivore at 74 to 82°F and pH 6.5 to 8.0, in 30 gallons for one fish and 40 or more for a pair, and it turns aggressive the moment it has a cave of eggs. People who have kept them will talk about dug-up plants, tankmates driven into the lid, and a pair that owns the tank. That is the practical review. A sheet that stops at the black bars will not mention how fast a 4 to 6 inch cichlid fills a 40-gallon tank with fry you then have to house.

A convict is satisfying when you wanted a tough Central American cichlid and gave it 30 gallons, caves, and no fragile tankmates. It is a regret when you wanted a community centerpiece. They live 8 to 10 years, eat pellets, bloodworms, brine shrimp, and earthworms, and they dig. Sand or fine gravel, hardy plants tied to rock, and filtration that can handle nitrate toward 40 ppm match the card. Get the adult temperament right in your head before you buy the striped juvenile. The fish will do exactly what a breeding convict does, and it will do it for most of a decade.

Crystal red shrimp eat biofilm first and prepared food second, and a new 10-gallon tank has little biofilm to offer. Caridina cantonensis of this grade need 68 to 72°F, pH about 5.8 to 6.6, general hardness 4 to 6 dGH, carbonate hardness 0 to 1 dKH, and TDS around 100 to 150 ppm, usually from remineralized RO water over an active substrate. Offer a tiny portion of a specialty shrimp food only after the moss and leaves already have a film, and remove leftovers the same day. Nitrate on this card is 10 ppm, tighter than a typical fish tank. A spoonful of fish flake will blow past that number and foul a molt in a species rated intermediate to advanced.

Variety for a crystal red is leaves, biofilm, and a rotation of fine shrimp foods, not a buffet of bloodworms. Indian almond leaves and alder cones support the acidic water and the grazing. A pellet from a shrimp line can fill gaps once the tank is mature. If a colony that used to pick across the moss ignores food and clusters near the surface, stop adding jars and check temperature, TDS, and ammonia. Loss of appetite in a 1 to 1.25 inch Caridina is an early crash signal. One complete-looking pellet cannot replace the film these shrimp were bred to graze in soft, acidic water.

Watch the picking, not a feeding frenzy. Healthy crystal reds work Java moss, Bucephalandra, and leaf litter continuously at 68 to 72°F. They do not school in the current for flakes. Drop a grain of food where you can see it and count how many shrimp arrive. A sudden pile of lifeless animals under the sponge filter, or a berried female who drops her eggs and stops grazing, is the behavior change that matters. Do not add aggressive feeders to make the tank look busy. These shrimp lose food and limbs to almost any fish with a mouth. The ecological role you can actually support is slow grazing on a mature, fish-free, or very carefully chosen setup.

A normal crystal red day is quiet grazing, the occasional clear molt, and females carrying eggs only when TDS and temperature have been steady. The bad day is a failed molt, a white ring, erratic swimming, or a colony that fades from red to pale after a top-off with the wrong water. Those signs are easy to miss in a 10-gallon tank full of moss unless you look on purpose. Copper and most fish medicines kill Caridina outright. Do not treat a hunch with an ich cure. If the group declines, check GH, KH, TDS, and temperature against the card, then ask a breeder of this line or a veterinarian. Guessing a dose is how the rest of the colony follows the first shrimp.

Quarantine new crystal reds in a cycled, buffered setup that already matches pH 5.8 to 6.6 and TDS 100 to 150, with a sponge filter and moss. A fish hospital tank is the wrong room. Residual copper, unstable KH, or a heater set to tropical fish temperatures will kill them while you watch. Drip-acclimate and give the group a few weeks so you can see molts, imported planaria, or a bacterial crash before it reaches the main colony. Add nothing medicinal on a schedule. The holding tank exists so a problem stays small. A 10-gallon display colony is intermediate to advanced because the water is narrow, not because the animals look delicate in a photo.

Let the active substrate and the sponge filter mature before the first crystal red goes in. Skipping the cycle, or rushing a tank that has not grown biofilm, is how an intermediate Caridina dies in a box that still tests like tap water. Wait until ammonia and nitrite are 0 ppm and the pH is sitting in the acidic band without daily crashes, at 68 to 72°F. KH near 0 to 1 means the substrate, not a box of crushed coral, is doing the buffering. A bottled bacteria product does not create leaf film. Patience is a seasoned 10-gallon tank. The shrimp are the last step, not the way you start the filter.

Budget for water, not for a fancier grade of red. Remineralized RO, tests for TDS, GH, and KH, an active substrate that eventually needs replacement, and specialty food are the repeating costs of a 10-gallon colony at 68 to 72°F. The shrimp's 1.5 to 2 year life is short, and the colony continues only if parameters stay put long enough to breed. People who buy high-grade animals and then top off with tap water lose them and buy again, which costs more than a cheap TDS meter. Plan on leaves, a spare sponge, and a thermometer you trust. The purchase price of the shrimp is the loud number and the small one.

Overheating is the heater story for crystal reds. The card wants 68 to 72°F, and a thermostat that sticks on can push a 10-gallon tank into the mid-70s in an afternoon, which these shrimp show as failed molts and a stall in breeding. A heater that fails off matters if the room falls far below the band, but many keepers run them without a heater in a stable room and do better. If you heat the tank, use a small wattage and a thermometer you read daily, not a powerful unit sized for a community tank. Filter failure is separate and serious. A dead sponge lets ammonia rise above 0 ppm, and Caridina die before you see the behavior change you were waiting for. Keep a spare sponge seeded, or you have nothing to swap in.

Buy buffering substrate, a sponge filter, and a TDS meter before you buy a higher grade of crystal red. The animals are intermediate to advanced because KH 0 to 1 and TDS 100 to 150 leave little room for sloppy gear. A hang-on-back filter with a strong intake sucks in shrimplets. A heater without a reliable thermostat cooks a colony that was supposed to stay at or under 72°F. The red pattern you paid for cannot be enjoyed if the hardware swings the water. Spend on the remineralizer and the substrate that hold the acidic band, and replace them when they are exhausted rather than when the colony has already crashed.

Cycle the tank before the zebra danios, and do not use the danios as the cycle. Danio rerio is a hardy 2-inch omnivore at 64 to 77°F, which makes people treat it as a disposable starter fish in an uncycled 10-gallon tank. That dumps ammonia onto a peaceful school that still has gills. Wait until tests show ammonia at 0 ppm, nitrite at 0 ppm, and nitrate near 20 ppm or under, with the heater, if you even need one, inside that cool band. A bottled bacteria product can help a fishless cycle. It is not a reason to add the school on day one. Beginner on this card means the finished tank is forgiving, not that the fish are a tool.

Zebra danios thrive on boring stability inside a wide band: 64 to 77°F, pH 6.0 to 8.0, 10 gallons or more, and a school that can sprint. They are peaceful omnivores. A pinch of flake they finish, plus the occasional frozen food, beats a constant rain of pellets that rot in a small tank. Quarantine new fish as a group. A lone danio in a box rushes the glass and will not show you a normal appetite. Ammonia at 0 ppm still matters, hardy reputation or not. The brand of flake is a smaller lever than a lid, because these fish jump when the school spooks.

Talk to someone who has kept zebra danios without turning them into cycle fodder. Ask how cool the room runs, because 64 to 77°F means many homes do not need a tropical heater, and a heater stuck at 82°F is a problem rather than a comfort. Ask about the school size in a 10-gallon tank and about jumpers on the floor. Keepers who have done it for the 3 to 5 year lifespan will mention lids and water changes, not a miracle food. That is the decision input. A fish sold as indestructible still needs a cycled tank and company.

A well-kept zebra danio is a fast, striped school in open water, at a temperature inside 64 to 77°F, eating a simple omnivore diet and not gasping at the surface. That is a genuinely fun fish for 3 to 5 years. The disappointing version is two pale survivors in a new tank that was never cycled, with a heater cranked far above the card. Peaceful and beginner are fair labels when the school and the water are in place. They are not an invitation to skip the test kit.

Discus eat often, and the water has to survive that habit. Symphysodon in a group need 82 to 88°F, pH 6.0 to 7.0, and very soft water, about 1 to 4 dGH, with nitrate held near 10 ppm and ideally closer to zero. Offer a protein-focused omnivore ration, a quality discus granule plus frozen or gel food, several small meals rather than one dump, in a tank of at least 55 gallons for five or six fish. Pull leftovers immediately. Ammonia and nitrite are marked critical, and a warm tank turns waste into those readings faster than a cool community. Ten gallons per adult is the working rule once the fish are no longer juveniles.

Rotate proteins so a discus group does not stall on a single frozen blend. A granule in the morning, a meaty frozen or gel feeding later, and a lighter day when the water is already due for a change covers an omnivore that still leans on protein. Watch the pecking order. A healthy group of five or six all comes forward. The fish that hangs at the back and refuses a food it ate yesterday is your early signal, often before the eye darkens or the body darkens. Do not answer that by adding three new foods. Test ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, and temperature. Appetite in a hierarchical, peaceful species is a status report.

Feed where you can see every fish. Discus are midwater cichlids from slow Amazon backwaters, and they should ease forward together at 82 to 88°F. Scatter the meal so the subordinate animal gets a share. A dominant fish that shoulders the others off a single pile is the social stress the group size is meant to dilute. Five or six is the minimum on this card for that reason. Target feeding with a pipette helps a thin fish without turning the tank into a competition. If the whole group refuses food and darkens, stop the feeding tricks and check the heater. At this temperature a failed thermostat shows up first as a missed meal.

Learn the group at feeding: eyes clear, bodies round without a pinched forehead, fins open, color even for the strain you keep. A discus that turns dark, clamps, breathes fast, or separates from the school has left that picture. White specks, frayed fins, and stringy feces are reasons to act while the fish still eats. Warm water at 82 to 88°F speeds both metabolism and disease. Look daily. This page is not a treatment recipe. If water tests show ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm and the fish still declines, call a veterinarian who sees discus. Do not run a home brew of remedies through a 55-gallon group.

Quarantine new discus at the same heat as the display, 82 to 88°F, in a cycled tank large enough for the group you bought. A cool hospital tub is a shock for a fish that lives this warm, and a single discus isolated from a hierarchical group often stops eating, which hides the problem. Several weeks of normal color and appetite is the bar before they join a resident group of five or six. Do not medicate on a calendar. If illness shows in quarantine, keep it out of the main tank and get veterinary guidance. A display at this temperature will spread whatever you add.

The useful opinion is from someone who has kept a discus group through a heater failure and a full set of water changes, not from a photo of a juvenile in a bare rack. Ask what temperature they actually hold, whether they can stay inside 82 to 88°F, and how they manage nitrate near 10 ppm. Advanced on this card is that workload plus soft water and a 55-gallon minimum. If the keeper you trust describes a fish that only colored up after the water got clean and the group got larger, you have a better decision tool than a price list.

Discus are satisfying when the group is calm, colored, and eating in soft water you test every day. They are a long disappointment when the tank cannot hold 82 to 88°F or when nitrate sits far above the 10 ppm line. Ten to 15 years is possible for Symphysodon that get a 55-gallon or larger home, five or six fish, and a protein-focused diet with the leftovers removed. Peaceful but hierarchical means you keep enough of them, not that any tankmate is welcome. Get those pieces right and the fish is as good as its reputation. Skip them and the reputation is the only thing left.

A decade with discus tracks the water changes and the heater, not the fixture you bought first. Hold 82 to 88°F, pH 6.0 to 7.0, and nitrate as close to the 10 ppm ceiling as you can manage, ideally nearer zero. Replace filter media on a schedule so a warm, heavily fed tank does not creep up in ammonia, which this card marks critical. The group of five or six in 55 gallons or more is the husbandry. A new light will not repair a fish that has been living in the wrong heat. In year eight the same boring tests are still the job.

Heater failure is the emergency this species is built around. Discus are listed at 82 to 88°F, and a single heater that dies during a cool night can drop a 55-gallon tank out of that band before morning. The fish darken, clamp, and stop eating, and ich finds them while they are down. A heater that sticks on and pushes past 88°F is the other failure, and it is just as serious in a tank you are also feeding heavily. Run two heaters, each able to hold the tank if the other quits, and a thermometer you read at feeding. If the filter stops, ammonia is critical at this temperature within hours, not days. A battery air pump buys oxygen during an outage. It does not hold 84°F or process the waste of a discus group.

Buy the second heater and the canister or sump before you buy a higher grade of discus. The fish are advanced, long-lived, and expensive to replace, and they share the tank with a bacteria colony that crashes if flow dies in 82 to 88°F water. A bargain heater with no backup is how a 10 to 15 year project ends in a weekend. Reliable gear costs less than a new group and a new cycle in a 55-gallon or larger tank. Service the o-rings and the impellers while the fish are healthy. The animals, the plants, and the mature filter are the value sitting in that warm water.

Dwarf crayfish pick and scavenge, and the food has to reach the floor of a tank that may be only 5 gallons.
