Cambarellus patzcuarensis takes sinking pellets, algae wafers, shrimp foods, and meaty bits such as bloodworm, brine shrimp, or daphnia, at 68 to 75°F. Feed a portion a small crayfish can finish, then remove the rest. Protein left in a nano tank becomes ammonia, and the card wants that reading at 0 ppm. They are not herbivores. A lettuce leaf is a snack, not the diet that supports a 1.5 to 2 inch animal through a 2 to 3 year life. Wild stocks from Lake Patzcuaro are endangered, so the food plan is for captive-bred orange crayfish, not a reason to collect from the lake.

Rotate plant and meat foods so you can see appetite against a known favorite. A wafer one evening and a bloodworm the next gives a CPO something to hunt and something to gnaw. If a crayfish that used to rush a worm now stays in a cave for days, test the water before you blame the brand. Refusal, a missed molt, or a crayfish that keeps falling onto its back are early trouble in an animal rated easy only when the tank is already stable. One pellet line will not cover a scavenger that also takes daphnia and algae film. Note what disappears. In a 5-gallon tank the uneaten half of a cube is the thing that fouls the next molt.

Feeding time is when a dwarf crayfish should leave the cave and search. Scatter a little bloodworm or a broken pellet across sand so it forages instead of finding a pile and guarding it. Two CPOs in a 5-gallon tank will fight over one food mound. Give 10 gallons or more for a group, with more than one cave, or the smaller animal never eats. They are less escape-prone than a big crayfish and they can still climb, so feed with the lid on your mind. A crayfish that no longer comes out for a food it used to claim is the health signal. Do not wait for it to die in the cave before you look at temperature and ammonia.

A healthy CPO explores, eats, and leaves a complete molt now and then at 68 to 75°F. The picture you do not want is a crayfish stuck halfway out of the old shell, lethargic in the open, or missing claws after a fight you did not give enough cover to prevent. Bacterial issues and bad molts follow dirty water and a temperature above the card's band. Look at feeding and again when the lights are low, because these animals are often out then. Copper, including many fish medicines, kills crayfish. Do not pour an ich treatment into their tank. If a molt fails or several animals die at once, check GH, KH, and ammonia, and ask a veterinarian rather than inventing a bath.

Quarantine a new dwarf crayfish alone, with a cave and a lid, in water already at 68 to 75°F and similar hardness to the display. They are small, but they will nip tankmates and each other, and a shared holding tank hides injuries as if they were disease. A few weeks of normal eating and one clean molt tells you the animal is worth adding to a 5-gallon or larger setup. Do not medicate that tub with a fish product. Copper residue is a death sentence for a CPO, and the main tank should be free of it too. Captive-bred orange crayfish are the animals to buy. Quarantine does not make a wild-caught lake animal a conservation plan.

The crayfish is the cheap part. A 5-gallon tank for one or two, or 10 gallons for a group, still needs sand, many small caves, a filter with a protected intake so babies are not sucked in, and food for a 2 to 3 year life. People who buy a vivid orange animal and a bowl later discover nitrate, escapes, and a heater they did not need until a hot room pushed the water past 75°F. Budget the lid, the test kit, and replacement filter sponges. Easy breeding on this card means juveniles you did not price. Plan the space before the first female carries eggs.

CPO crayfish are a cool-water animal, listed at 68 to 75°F. A heater that fails on is the common disaster, especially in 5 gallons, where a stuck thermostat can leave the card's range in a few hours and trigger bad molts. A heater that fails off only matters if the room drops well below 68°F. Many keepers do better with no heater and a stable room than with a powerful unit borrowed from a tropical tank. If you heat, use low wattage and read the thermometer daily. Filter failure is the other half. A clogged sponge in a small box lets ammonia rise above 0 ppm, and a crayfish in a cave dies out of sight. Keep a second sponge running somewhere so you can swap it in.

Spend on a tight lid, a guarded filter intake, and a thermometer before you spend on a brighter orange bloodline. Dwarf crayfish breed readily, live 2 to 3 years, and will stock a 5-gallon tank with juveniles that a naked intake destroys. A heater sized for a 40-gallon community tank is the wrong tool in a box that should stay at or under 75°F. Caves, sand, and plants they only nibble are the habitat. Reliable small gear protects that setup and the captive-bred animals in it. Replace a tired air pump while the crayfish are still coming out to feed, not after the water has gone stale.

Finish the cycle before a dwarf gourami sees the tank. These are 3.5-inch labyrinth fish, peaceful omnivores at 72 to 82°F and pH 6.0 to 7.5, and the 10-gallon minimum is already a small volume for an ammonia spike. Test until ammonia is 0 ppm, nitrite is 0 ppm, and nitrate sits near 20 ppm or below. A newly filled tank, even with a bottle of bacteria and a picture of a flame gourami on the box, is the wrong moment to add the fish. They breathe air at the surface, so leave a gap of humid air under the lid. That does not let them survive nitrite. Beginner describes a cycled planted tank, not a weekend setup.

A dwarf gourami needs stable water, food at the surface and just below it, and a quarantine that acknowledges how many of these fish arrive already sick. Hold 72 to 82°F, pH 6.0 to 7.5, and a peaceful community that will not nip the feelers. Feed an omnivore flake or small pellet they can take from the top, plus frozen food a couple of times a week, in a 10-gallon or larger tank. Quarantine every new gourami. Dwarf gourami iridovirus is widespread in the hobby, it has no home cure, and a fish that is already thin or hanging at the surface should not go straight into your display. Chemistry and appetite tell you more than the color name on the label.

Ask keepers what happened to their dwarf gouramis after the first month, not how bright the male was in the shop. This species is listed at 4 to 6 years and beginner, and a lot of fish never get there because of iridovirus and because they were added to uncycled 10-gallon tanks. People who have kept them well will talk about quarantine, surface access, and calm tankmates. People who lost three in a row are telling you the sourcing problem. Use that conversation. A peaceful omnivore at 72 to 82°F is a fair project only if you can walk away from a fish that will not eat.

The satisfying dwarf gourami is a male in good weight, feelers intact, working a planted 10-gallon tank at 72 to 82°F and coming to the surface on his own terms. That fish exists, and a 4 to 6 year life is on the card for a reason. It is not the hollow, dark animal hovering in the corner of a shop tank. Choose a fish that eats, quarantine it, and keep ammonia at 0 ppm. Do that and a peaceful gourami is one of the better small centerpiece fish. Skip the quarantine and the color is often all you get.

Electric blue acaras feed in the middle of the tank and along the bottom, with less of the nonstop sifting a ram does and less of the lunging a big terror does. In 30 gallons or more, offer a pellet and a frozen food where a 6 to 7 inch cichlid can take it without being mobbed, and watch whether both fish in a pair eat. They are peaceful for a cichlid, not peaceful next to a frantic school that steals every cube. Scatter part of the meal so a subordinate animal gets some. If one acara stops coming up while the other guards a corner, you are seeing pair stress or illness, and the feeding pattern is the clue. Live and frozen foods keep them searching. A single pile under a decoration only feeds the bolder fish.

Portions should match a 6 to 7 inch omnivore, not a pile meant for a fish twice that length. A cichlid pellet they can chew, plus bloodworm or brine shrimp, in amounts finished within a few minutes, keeps a 30-gallon tank from climbing in nitrate. The card's food range of about 50 to 150 dollars a year is plenty for that rotation. Overfeeding is the usual failure with a fish this calm, because it looks like it is always hungry and the keeper keeps pouring. A sunken belly is the other failure, usually a fish losing food to a tankmate. Feed so you can see the blue fish swallow. Eight to 10 years is a long time to get the amount wrong.

Use more than one food so a missed meal means something. Pellet, frozen brine, and an occasional earthworm or bloodworm give an electric blue acara a varied omnivore diet and give you a favorite item to test appetite against. A fish that refuses the worm it usually takes, and fades from bright blue toward gray, is an early health signal in a species that can look dramatic even when it is declining. Do not answer with a new jar every day. Note the refusal, test the water, and look at the fins. Variety is a tool for observation on a beginner-to-intermediate cichlid, not a shopping project.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress show on an electric blue acara as white grains on the blue, ragged fins, redness, or a fish that has gone dark and stopped coming to food. Clean water and a calm tank are the prevention that fits a cichlid listed as peaceful for its family. A 30-gallon tank with constant harassment will produce the stress half of that list. Quarantine new fish for a few weeks before they meet a resident pair. Keep medications out of the plan until you know what you are treating. This card does not list a dose, and aquarium salt is not a complete answer. If the fish declines in clean water, ask a veterinarian.

Watch the blue at feeding. A healthy electric blue acara should be bright, fins spread, taking food in the open of a 30-gallon or larger tank. Your baseline is that brightness and the way the fish moves, not a generic cichlid posture. A sudden dark wash, a clamped fin, rapid breathing, or a refusal over several days is the deviation. White spot stands out on this color if you actually look, which is an advantage over a muddy green fish. Use the daily feed as the exam. A fish that has stopped eating among decorations is hard to catch later, so act while it still comes forward, and do not invent a treatment dose.

Quarantine electric blue acaras in a cycled tank with a cave and open space, held near the same conditions as the display, before they go into a 30-gallon community. They are peaceful for a cichlid and still territorial enough that a sick newcomer in the display means rearranging rocks to net it. Several weeks of bright color and steady eating is the observation you want. Do not medicate because the fish is new and blue fish sometimes arrive stressed. If ich appears, it stays in the quarantine tank, and a veterinarian sets any treatment. The display, especially with other species, should not be your experiment.

Lay out a South American cichlid tank, not a rift-lake pile. Electric blue acaras use open sand, a cave, wood, and plants that can take some digging, in 30 gallons or more. They are peaceful for a cichlid, so the scape should give a pair a corner without turning the whole tank into a fortress that traps timid tankmates. Shift a single piece if a fish is pacing a reflection. Do not rebuild the layout weekly. A pair that knows where the cave is spends its time in the blue you bought it for, instead of re-digging a new map every Sunday.

Scatter frozen food across the sand and let an electric blue acara search, then offer a pellet it can take in the water column. That mix matches an omnivore of 6 to 7 inches and gives you two ways to see appetite. Live foods from a clean source extend the hunt. They are not required every day. A fish that will no longer move for a scattered feeding has left the behavior you are using as a health check. On an 8 to 10 year cichlid, that change is worth a water test the same evening.

Buy electric blue acaras from a shop that can show you the fish eating and that keeps the tank clear, or from a seller with a live-arrival guarantee. The card's range of about 5 to 100 dollars per fish means color and size vary, and a cheap faded fish is not a bargain if it will not eat. Avoid tanks with white spots and torn fins. Quarantine on arrival. A beginner-to-intermediate cichlid still deserves a healthy start, and the blue only stays interesting when the animal was in good condition on day one.

Use the card's figures as the floor, not the whole story. Setup runs about 100 to 500 dollars or more, the fish about 5 to 100 dollars, yearly upkeep about 200 to 500 dollars, and food about 50 to 150 dollars, for a 6 to 7 inch cichlid that needs 30 gallons and can live 8 to 10 years. People who buy the color and delay the filter service end up with ich, fin rot, and a second purchase. Add media, a spare heater, and test kits to the yearly number. A peaceful cichlid is not a low-waste fish. The blue you are paying for fades in a dirty tank just as fast as any other color.

A 30-gallon tank cools and heats faster than the big cichlid tanks people compare it with. If the heater fails off, an electric blue acara drops out of a stable tropical range overnight and often stops eating. If it fails on, the same volume overshoots and the fish darkens and gasps. Either swing is a common door into ich and bacterial trouble for a fish that otherwise behaves well. Read the thermometer daily. Keep a backup heater sized for 30 gallons and a way to aerate if the filter quits. An air pump during a power cut helps oxygen. It does not process the waste of a 7-inch cichlid, so plan a water change once power returns if the filter has been off for hours.

A controllable heater and a filter you can open without destroying the aquascape are the gear that fits this fish. Electric blue acaras can be modest in price and still sit in a planted 30-gallon tank that took months to settle, alongside tankmates that are part of the same cost. A no-name heater is a weak place to save across an 8 to 10 year life. Buy equipment you can get parts for, and replace a noisy impeller before it stops. The fish is peaceful for a cichlid, which means the community around it is also yours to protect when a pump fails.

An electric blue crayfish is a nighttime scavenger with a large appetite for a 4 to 5 inch animal. Procambarus alleni takes sinking pellets, algae wafers, shrimp pellets, and meat such as bloodworm, earthworm, feeder shrimp, or a piece of fish, at 65 to 75°F in 20 gallons or more. Feed after the lights drop, in a portion that is gone by morning, and remove anything still there. Leftover fish flesh in a warm corner will push ammonia above 0 ppm and nitrate toward the card's 40 ppm ceiling. This is not a vegetable pet. Plants are something it shreds, not the diet that carries a 5 to 6 year life. One crayfish is the stocking. A second one turns feeding into a fight.

Alternate a wafer, a worm, and a bit of shrimp so you can tell boredom from illness. A crayfish that ignores a new pellet but still takes an earthworm is being selective. A crayfish that refuses the worm, stays buried, and skips a molt is not. Electric blue crayfish are rated easy when the water is stable, and they still decline fast after a bad water change or a temperature above 75°F. Write down what was eaten overnight. One commercial food will not replace the mix of carrion and plant matter this Florida species picks through in the wild, and it will not warn you when appetite collapses.

Put the food in the open sand and watch from across the room. A settled electric blue crayfish will come out, drag a worm to a cave, and eat. If it never leaves the PVC pipe, either the room is too bright or the animal is off. Do not tap the glass to force a show. Two crayfish in one 20-gallon tank will not politely share that worm. The larger one eats, and the smaller one loses claws. Feed as foraging, with the lid already closed, because this species is an excellent climber and a feeding session is when people leave the top off. A crayfish that abandons a favorite food is the signal to test ammonia and temperature, not to offer a larger portion.

Healthy electric blues explore at night, eat, and shed a complete shell now and then at 65 to 75°F. Worry when the shell splits and the animal cannot back out, when it sits in the open during the day and will not threaten a tong, or when the blue fades to a dull gray after a move. Injuries from bare-tank fights and bacterial problems after dirty water are the common pattern, not a mystery disease. Look at night, when they are actually active. Copper and copper-based fish medicines kill crayfish. Never use them in this tank. If a molt stalls or the animal stops eating for several days in clean water, ask a veterinarian instead of dosing a hunch.

Quarantine an electric blue crayfish by itself in a lidded, cycled tank with a cave, at 65 to 75°F, before it meets fish or another crayfish. It is predatory. Small fish and shrimp are food, and a shared quarantine box becomes a crime scene you then misread as infection. A few weeks of eating and one successful molt is enough to see that the animal is sound. Add no fish medication to that tub. The display should also be free of copper residue from any earlier ich treatment, or the new crayfish dies on contact. A tight lid belongs on the quarantine tank too. They leave through airline gaps.

Price the adult setup, not the bright juvenile. Twenty gallons is the minimum for a single 4 to 5 inch crayfish that lives 5 to 6 years, destroys most plants, and needs a filter strong enough that nitrate can be managed toward 40 ppm. People buy the color, add a handful of expensive plants, and then buy the plants again. Budget a real lid, PVC or caves, sinking food, and replacement filter parts. Easy breeding on this card means babies you must separate, because the adults will eat them. That is a second container, not a bonus. The livestock price is the small line on an animal that will try to leave the tank.

This crayfish is a cool-water Florida species, listed at 65 to 75°F, and a heater that sticks on is the failure that hurts it. In 20 gallons a runaway thermostat can push the tank well above 75°F in a day, and the animal responds with a bad molt or a refusal to come out. A heater that dies in a mild room often does nothing harmful, because 65°F is still inside the card. Use heat only if the room actually falls below that, and use a small wattage with a thermometer you check. Filter failure is less forgiving. A burrower sitting in a pocket of stale water meets ammonia above 0 ppm while the surface still looks fine. Keep a spare sponge or a backup pump. The lid does not help if the water underneath is toxic.

Buy the lid and the filter before you buy a deeper shade of blue. Electric blue crayfish escape, shred plants, and produce enough waste that a 20-gallon tank needs equipment you can trust for 5 to 6 years. A loose hood is how they dry out on the floor. An intake without a guard eats juveniles if you let them breed. A tropical heater cranked for tetras cooks an animal that should stay at or below 75°F. Spend on those pieces and on a cave that will not leach copper. The color form is a captive line of Procambarus alleni. It is only worth keeping if the hardware lets it stay in the tank and in the right temperature.

Yellow labs graze. Labidochromis caeruleus picks at aufwuchs on rock, and in a 30-gallon or larger tank the feeding that matches that habit is a spirulina flake or pellet rubbed into the rock, plus a small portion of frozen food, not a pile of shrimp in open water. They are peaceful for mbuna, which is a low bar, and two males will still argue over one food spot. Spread the meal along the rock so several fish can graze at once. A lab that will not leave its cave when food hits the stone is either dominated or ill. Watch that difference. A fish being chased off the rock needs a different layout. A fish that ignores food entirely needs a water test. Hunting bloodworms all day is the wrong enrichment for a mbuna and a good way to bring on bloat.

Feed these 4 to 5 inch cichlids like the herbivores they are. A spirulina-based pellet, a vegetable wafer, and only a modest meaty item keep an electric yellow inside the diet that Malawi mbuna actually do well on. The card allows about 50 to 150 dollars a year for food, which covers a vegetable staple if you are not buying a high-protein carnivore stick. Overfeeding protein is a known way this species fades, swells, and stops eating. Underfeeding shows up as a thin fish losing the rock to pushier mbuna. Offer small meals they finish. Six to 10 years is long enough for a bad menu to matter more than the yellow you bought.

A vegetable pellet, a spirulina flake, and a rare frozen treat are enough variety. You are not building a seafood rotation for a predator. The point of changing foods is to notice the day a yellow lab refuses the pellet it usually rasps off your fingers or off the rock. That refusal, with a darker wash or a fish hiding while the others graze, is an early illness sign in a beginner mbuna that people assume is indestructible. Test the water and look at the belly before you enrich the menu with more protein. Appetite for the herbivore staple is the signal. A new jar of bloodworms is not the test.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress still happen to electric yellows, usually when a new fish is dumped into a crowded rock pile or the water swings. White grains on a yellow body are easy to see if you look, which is a gift this color gives you. Fin rot and a dark, clamped fish follow chasing and poor water. Quarantine newcomers for a few weeks. They are peaceful for mbuna and still live in a tank where you may not want to dose anything while other fish are present. Do not keep a broad medicine as a reflex, and do not invent a salt dose. If the lab stops grazing in clean water, ask a veterinarian.

The daily look is the rock at feeding. A healthy yellow lab should be out, bright, rasping, fins down in a normal posture rather than clamped. Males and females are both yellow in this species, so you cannot use color alone to excuse a fish that has gone pale. Rapid breathing, a sunken belly, white specks, or a lab glued to the back glass while the others eat are the changes that count. Learn your group for a week and the odd one stands out. Catch problems while the fish still takes spirulina. A mbuna deep in the rockwork, off food, is a surgery of a catch, and this page will not give you a dose to pour in while you decide.

Quarantine yellow labs in alkaline, hard water that resembles the display, with a rock to graze, before they enter a 30-gallon mbuna tank. A soft-water hospital tub is the wrong chemistry for a Lake Malawi fish, and it will stress them into the illness you are trying to detect. Keep the group or the new individual there for a few weeks of normal grazing. They are peaceful for mbuna, so a bare, screaming tank of other cichlids is a poor quarantine neighbor. No calendar of medications. If ich shows up, it stays in that second tank and a veterinarian guides any treatment. Your display rock pile is a terrible place to start an experiment.

Stack rock the way a mbuna uses it. Electric yellows want caves, sight-line breaks, and surfaces they can graze, in 30 gallons or more, with open sand only as a lane between the rock. They are among the calmer Malawi cichlids and they still need a territory each. Rearranging the entire pile every week resets those borders and starts fights you then blame on the species. Add a rock if a fish is homeless. Leave the rest of the map alone. Sharp, thin decor cuts a bolting lab. Texas holey rock or similar rounded holes fit this fish better than a shelf of glass ornaments.

Enrichment that fits a yellow lab is grazing, not a hunt. Paste a spirulina gel on the rock or clip a piece of blanched zucchini where they have to pick at it through the day. That keeps the aufwuchs behavior and tells you who is willing to come out. A cube of bloodworm is a treat at most, not the activity. If the labs stop working a food they usually rasp, treat it as a health check and test the tank. A 4 to 5 inch mbuna that abandons the rock is not bored. It is off.

Buy electric yellows from a shop whose Malawi tanks are clear, alkaline, and not a bag of mixed unidentified mbuna, or from a seller with a live-arrival guarantee. The card's fish price of about 5 to 100 dollars tracks size and quality. Ask to see them eat a vegetable food. A yellow lab that will only chase frozen shrimp in the shop has been trained onto the wrong menu. Refuse spotted, thin, or torn fish. Quarantine in hard water. A beginner mbuna is beginner only when the animal you bring home is already grazing.

The card's setup range of about 100 to 500 dollars or more, fish at about 5 to 100 dollars, yearly costs around 200 to 500 dollars, and food around 50 to 150 dollars assume a 30-gallon or larger rock tank for a 6 to 10 year cichlid. A yellow lab is often the first mbuna people buy, and the expensive surprise is the second tank when the group outgrows the minimum or the filter cannot keep up. Budget crushed coral or a buffer if your tap water is soft, plus a spare heater. Cutting food quality to save the 50 dollar end of that food range is how a herbivore ends up on a bargain high-protein pellet. Spend the food money on spirulina.

Malawi tanks are warm, and a yellow lab in 30 gallons feels a heater failure quickly. If the unit dies in a cold room, grazing stops and ich often follows a chill in a fish that had been stable. If the unit sticks on, the same small volume overheats, oxygen drops, and a peaceful-for-mbuna group starts gasping at the surface and then fighting. Read the thermometer on the glass every day. Keep a second heater that can hold 30 gallons, and a way to move water if the filter stops. An air stone in a power cut keeps oxygen up for a few hours. It does not replace biological filtration on a rock pile of cichlids that are fed daily. Change water once the filter has been down long enough to stall.

A heater with a working thermostat and a filter rated for a messy mbuna tank matter more than a color-enhancing light. Electric yellows can be inexpensive on the card's 5 to 100 dollar scale and still live 6 to 10 years in a rockscape that took real time to stack and cycle. That scape, and any other Malawi fish in it, is what a cheap heater destroys. Buy gear you can replace parts for. A cracked impeller on a Friday night is a worse surprise than a plain fixture. The fish is beginner by mbuna standards only when the equipment can hold hard, alkaline, warm water without a weekly crisis.

Ember tetras stay bright orange when the school is together and the water is left alone. They are 0.8-inch peaceful nano fish with a 2 to 4 year life, and the card starts the tank at 10 gallons. Keep ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm, feed a fine omnivore portion they can finish, and quarantine new embers as a group. A single tiny tetra in a bare cup fades to beige and will not eat, so you learn nothing about disease. Chemistry and a real school do more than any bottled polish. Beginner is fair only after the 10-gallon tank is cycled and planted enough that the group will come out.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress show on ember tetras as a school that turns pale, flicks, clamps, or carries white grains you can barely see on an orange body. A 10-gallon tank makes those problems move fast when a feeding is too heavy. Quarantine the new school for a few weeks before it joins other nano fish. Do not stage aquarium salt and a broad medicine as the plan. This card lists no dose, and a 0.8-inch fish is easy to kill with a remedy measured for something larger. If the group declines, ask a veterinarian and fix the water first.

Give ember tetras plants, dimmer light, and a little open water, in the spirit of a small soft-water creek rather than a bare glass box. Ten gallons is the minimum for a peaceful school, and it fills up if you stack hardscape to the surface. Change a dying stem. Do not tear the scape apart on a schedule or the orange group spends a week hiding instead of schooling. Shade and fine leaves are the habitat. Novelty is a lower priority than a layout they already know how to use.

Rinse baby brine or a crushed micro pellet through the plants and let the embers pick it out. That is the hunt a 0.8-inch tetra can actually perform, and it is how you count a school that otherwise disappears into moss. Large bloodworms are the wrong enrichment. They foul a 10-gallon tank and the fish cannot take them. When the picking stops and the orange dulls, test the water the same day. Feeding behavior is the early sign on a fish whose body is too small to show much else.

Choose ember tetras from a shop that keeps a colored school in clean water, or from a seller who guarantees live arrival. The card spans about 5 to 100 dollars per fish, so you are paying for condition and group size as much as for the name. Walk past pale, clamped fish. Acclimate the school into a cycled quarantine together. A beginner nano tetra that arrives sick uses up a 2 to 4 year lifespan before you have learned the tank. Buy the group, not a single specimen for a photo.

Endlers need hard, stable water and a plan for babies, more than they need a special flake. Poecilia wingei males stay about an inch and females about an inch and a half, live 2 to 3 years, and do well at 72 to 82°F, pH 7.0 to 8.5, and general hardness 10 to 25 dGH. The tank floor is 5 gallons, with 10 or more a better colony size. They are peaceful, active omnivores. Feed a little, often enough that males still have energy to display, and quarantine new fish away from guppies if you care about an N-class or P-class line. K-class fish are already guppy hybrids. A bottle of tonic will not keep a pure line pure, and it will not keep nitrate near 30 ppm in a colony that is breeding.

Two or three years with Endlers is a colony problem, not a gear problem. Keep 72 to 82°F and hard water, give them plants for fry cover, and decide before the first brood whether you are keeping a pure Laguna de Patos line or a mixed tank. Wild fish are critically endangered. Aquarium stocks matter, and dumping hybrids back into a story about conservation does not help. A sponge filter and a lid outperform a new light. Nitrate can run toward 30 ppm on this card and still needs water changes once juveniles appear. The husbandry that lasts is the water plus a decision about how many fish you are willing to house.

Cycle for the waste of the adult fancy, not for a small slim-bodied feeder. A 6 to 8 inch fancy goldfish needs 20 gallons of its own, at 65 to 75°F and pH 6.0 to 8.0, and an uncycled filter under that body is an ammonia spike measured in hours. Wait until ammonia and nitrite read 0 ppm and you can hold nitrate near 20 ppm with water changes that match how much you feed. Do not add the fish to cycle the tank, and do not add two fancies to a 20-gallon box because the minimum was written per fish. A bacteria bottle can start a fishless cycle. It does not shrink the adult. Beginner water chemistry is still chemistry. The gallon rule is the part people skip.

Fancy goldfish welfare is oxygen, a cool band, and food that sinks. Hold 65 to 75°F. A tropical heater set for tetras is already too hot, and warm water holds less oxygen for a deep-bodied fish that gulps at the surface. Feed a sinking omnivore pellet so they are not taking air with floating flakes, which is a common path to buoyancy trouble in fancies. Quarantine new goldfish in cool water, not in a hospital tank at 82°F. They often arrive with parasites from crowded systems, and a hot dip is not on this card. Ammonia at 0 ppm in 20 gallons per fish matters more than the brand of gel food.

A fancy goldfish that gets 20 gallons to itself, 65 to 75°F, and a filter you actually clean will use the 10 to 15 year lifespan on the card. That is a round-bodied fish cruising, eating sinking pellets, and not gasping. It asks for a real water-change habit, because the waste of an 8-inch omnivore does not care that the species is labeled beginner. If you can keep nitrate near 20 ppm and resist the urge to add tropical tankmates that need hotter water, the fish is a good long project. If the tank is a bowl, the lifespan on the card is someone else's fish.

Fiddler crabs are brackish land animals that visit the water, and treating them as freshwater fish is how they die. Uca needs a paludarium of 10 gallons or more, half or more of it above the waterline, shallow water they can leave, sand they can burrow in, 75 to 85°F, humidity above 75 percent, and a specific gravity around 1.005 to 1.015 with pH 8.0 to 8.3. Feed a measured crab pellet or sinking food on the land edge, and quarantine new crabs in brackish water, not in a freshwater cup. A lid is part of welfare. They are escape experts. Stable salinity and a damp burrow do more than any freshwater conditioner poured into a tank they should not be living in.

Decide on fiddler crabs only after you have seen the paludarium, not the crab in a dry souvenir tank. You need land, shallow brackish water, heat for both, and a lid. Keepers who have held them for the 2 to 3 year lifespan will talk about humidity crashes and about crabs that drowned in water that was too deep or dried out on land that was too hot. Breeding is very difficult and is not a reason to buy them. If the person you trust is keeping them in a freshwater community with tetras, you are hearing a short story. The card says brackish. Believe the card over a shop label that says freshwater crab.

A fiddler that is out at the surface, feeding, waving a large claw, and retreating into a damp burrow is the animal worth keeping. That takes 75 to 85°F, humidity, and specific gravity 1.005 to 1.015, with a 10-gallon or larger paludarium and a lid that actually latches. It is a satisfying oddball when those pieces exist. It is a dead crab in a freshwater fish tank or in an open bowl on a desk. Moderate care on this card means the land-and-water build, not a difficult diet. Get the brackish paludarium right and the claw-waving is the show. Skip it and there is no second act.

A flowerhorn is a single, highly aggressive hybrid that needs the tank finished before the fish arrives. Plan on 75 gallons at the minimum, more for a 10 to 16 inch adult, 80 to 86°F, pH 7.0 to 8.0, and filtration oversized for the waste of a carnivore-leaning omnivore. The commitment is bare or sandy decor they will rearrange, a tight lid, and meals of a quality pellet plus shrimp, earthworm, or similar, with leftovers removed. Ten to 12 years is a long time to keep a fish that should not have cichlid roommates and must never be released. Released flowerhorns are already invasive in some tropical waters. If you can hold that heat and that temperament, the hump and the interaction are the reward. If you wanted a community tank, this is the wrong fish.

French angelfish welfare is a big, stable reef or fish-only system and a quarantine that happens before the fish ever sees coral. Pomacanthus adults reach about 15 inches, live 10 to 15 years, and the card wants 250 gallons, 72 to 82°F, pH 8.1 to 8.4, specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, and nitrate near 10 ppm. They are semi-aggressive omnivores. Feed a marine angel preparation that includes sponge and algae matter plus meaty foods, and do not expect a juvenile diet to stay appropriate for the adult. New fish belong in a separate marine tank long enough to show appetite and to reveal marine ich or velvet. Copper, if a veterinarian uses it, stays in that fish-only tank. It does not go into a display with invertebrates. Measured feeding and salinity you actually test beat any bottle of reef potion.

Two hundred and fifty gallons, expert care, and a semi-aggressive adult angel are the commitment, not the cute juvenile banded pattern. If you can hold 72 to 82°F and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, run a skimmer and live rock, and keep a lid and a filter sized for a 15-inch omnivore, a French angelfish can be a remarkable 10 to 15 year fish. It will sample corals and intimidate timid tankmates. The card is explicit that beginners without a mature tank, and very shy species, are a poor match. Do the adult tank first. The juvenile in a smaller box is a temporary loan with a deadline, and the deadline is the fish's growth.

Frontosa are a big, slow Tanganyikan cichlid, and the variables that matter are alkaline water, a 75-gallon or larger tank, and new fish that have been watched before they join a group. Adults reach 12 to 14 inches and can live 15 to 25 years. They are peaceful only by the standard of large cichlids. Anything that fits in the mouth is still a meal, so tiny tankmates are food, not dither. Feed a measured carnivore-leaning ration at lights-down, when these fish actually hunt, and keep ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm. A brand of buffer does less than a finished cycle and a cave for each big head in the group.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress show on frontosa as white spots on a dark body, eroded fins, or a fish that will not leave the cave at feeding time. They are intermediate to advanced largely because the adult is huge and the group is a long commitment, not because the juvenile is fragile in the shop. Keep the 75-gallon tank clean and do not chill them. Quarantine new frontosa for a few weeks in hard, alkaline water. A soft-water hospital tank is the wrong room for a Tanganyikan fish and will stress it into the symptoms you hoped to avoid. No dose is printed on this card. If the fish declines, ask a veterinarian rather than salting a 75-gallon tank by guess.

Have the large tank, the rock caves, and the filter in place before you buy a frontosa. A juvenile hump is not the adult. Twelve to 14 inches and 15 to 25 years means the setup range on the card, about 100 to 500 dollars or more, is often only a down payment on a tank that can hold a group. Talk to keepers who have kept them past the first upgrade. They will mention deep-looking rock, dimmer light, and the fish that disappeared into a neighbor's mouth. Read that as stocking advice. A peaceful giant still needs a home sized for the giant.

Build caves and open sand in the Tanganyikan pattern, with rock that will not collapse when a 12-inch fish leans on it. Frontosa hover near cover and come out on their own schedule. Rearranging the pile every week destroys the map and stresses a fish you bought for its calm. Add a cave if a new animal has nowhere to stand. Leave a stable structure alone otherwise. Sharp plastic is a cut waiting for a startled giant. The habitat is heavy rock and room, in 75 gallons at the absolute floor and more if you keep a real group.

Feed frontosa at dusk, a sinking pellet or a prawn they can take near the cave, and let them hunt rather than chasing flakes at the surface in bright light. Frozen or fresh meaty foods from a clean source match a fish that eats smaller animals in the lake. The enrichment and the health check are the same moment. A frontosa that will not come out for a prawn it usually takes has left its baseline. Test the water while the fish is still willing to show itself. A 14-inch cichlid off food, deep in the rock, is a difficult patient.

Buy frontosa from a shop that keeps them in hard alkaline water and can show you a fish eating, or from a seller with a live-arrival guarantee and a record you can read. Prices on the card run about 5 to 100 dollars, and a juvenile at the low end still becomes the same 12 to 14 inch adult. Refuse thin fish and any tank sprinkled with white spot. Quarantine in similar chemistry to the display. A peaceful giant that arrives sick costs the yearly upkeep, about 200 to 500 dollars on this card, in problems before you have enjoyed the hump.

Ghost shrimp are a short-lived scavenger, and the welfare is clean water plus a quarantine that treats them as livestock rather than as disposable feeders. Palaemonetes paludosus stays about 1.5 to 2 inches, lives 1 to 1.5 years, and needs 5 gallons or more at 70 to 80°F, pH 7.0 to 8.0, with general hardness around 5 to 15 dGH. They eat detritus and a little algae, so a mature tank with a sinking pellet is the feeding plan. Ammonia and nitrite stay at 0 ppm. Nitrate can run toward 30 ppm and still needs a water change in a small box. New shrimp should sit in a separate cycled tank, because feeder tanks often carry problems, and copper from a previous fish treatment will kill them. A sponge filter protects adults and any larvae. The brand of pellet matters less than not poisoning the tank they have to molt in.

German blue rams pick through sand the way a shorebird works a flat, and that search is the behavior a 20-gallon tank should allow. Mikrogeophagus ramirezi is a 2 to 3 inch peaceful cichlid with only 3 to 4 years on the clock, so a pair that never gets to sift has lost a large piece of a short life. Offer fine foods on the sand after bossier tankmates have eaten, or the rams simply do not get the meal. Scatter brine or daphnia instead of parking a cube in one hole. If one ram hovers and the other sifts, look at bullying or illness before you add more food. They are intermediate because the water and the warmth have to be right, not because the feeding trick is complicated.

Small meals, warm water, and leftovers removed: that is the feeding discipline for a fish this size. A soft pellet, baby brine, and a little frozen daphnia, finished in a minute, suit a 2 to 3 inch omnivore better than cichlid sticks. The card's yearly food figure of about 50 to 150 dollars buys quality small foods if you resist the jumbo jar. Uneaten protein in a warm planted tank becomes nitrate fast, and rams show it by fading and clamping. Feed a young pair lightly and often. Skip the next round when the sand is still dirty with worms. Three to 4 years leaves no time for a chronically overfed or underfed fish.

Keep two or three foods in the rotation so a refusal means something on a ram. Pellet one day, brine the next, daphnia later in the week. A German blue ram that turns its nose up at brine but still takes pellet may be full or spawning. A ram that refuses all three, loses the blue and the red belly, and stops sifting is an early sick fish. These are less forgiving than Bolivian rams, which is why the difficulty says intermediate. Write the food and the response down. Guessing from memory is how a 3-year fish slips away between water changes.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and plain stress are the list that actually kills German blue rams, often after a chill or a dirty week. White spot, ragged fins, and a dark clamped pair are the visible end of that list. The prevention that matches this species is very clean, warm, stable water and no constant harassment in the 20-gallon tank. Quarantine new arrivals for a few weeks. They are peaceful and they are not tough. Do not stock a remedy shelf and call it readiness. This card has no dose, and salt plus a broad medicine is how a small sensitive cichlid gets burned. If the pair fades in water that tests clean, call a veterinarian.

Look at the sand when you feed. A healthy German blue ram should be bright, belly showing color, face down, chewing. That is the baseline, and it is different from a Bolivian ram mostly in how quickly it disappears when the water is wrong. A fish that faces the glass, breathes hard, or looks hollow over two or three days has left the baseline. White grains show well on the blue body if the light is on and you are actually watching. Use that minute. A ram off food among plants is miserable to net later, so act while it still comes out, and leave dosing to a veterinarian.

Quarantine German blue rams warm, in a cycled tank with sand, as a pair if they came together. A cool bare tub will shut their appetite down and you will learn nothing. They are peaceful, short-lived, and intermediate in difficulty, so the few weeks of watching them sift is not optional ceremony. Only move them to the 20-gallon display when color and appetite are steady. If white spot appears, it stays in quarantine. Do not pour a treatment into the display because a forum listed one. Get a veterinarian's plan, and keep every other fish out of the experiment.

Cycle and heat the 20-gallon tank before you shop for rams. German blue rams are the sensitive cousin in this genus, and a fresh box with a swinging temperature is a common way to waste a 3 to 4 year lifespan in the first month. Setup on the card is about 100 to 500 dollars or more, and a fish can run about 5 to 100 dollars. Spend it on a ready tank, a reliable heater, and sand. Keepers who have kept this species, as opposed to Bolivian rams, will talk about warmth and water changes. Listen for that. A general beginner-fish thread will steer you wrong.

Fine sand, a low cave, and plants tied to wood suit a German blue ram better than a rock pile built for mbuna. They sift and they spawn on a flat stone or a leaf, in 20 gallons or more. Digging is normal. Uprooting a garden you just replanted every week is optional and stressful for a peaceful pair. Change one dead plant. Leave the spawning site alone if a pair has chosen it. The aquascape should make the sifting easy to see, because that behavior is how you judge the fish. A cave they can hover under beats a stack of ornaments they cannot use.

Scatter live or frozen baby brine across the sand and let the rams hunt grain by grain. That is the enrichment that fits a 2 to 3 inch dwarf, and it is also the exam. A pellet still feeds them on ordinary days. It does not show you the face-down search. When a German blue ram will not hunt a food it chased yesterday, test temperature and nitrogen the same hour. On a fish that may only live 3 or 4 years, waiting for a dramatic symptom wastes a large fraction of the life.

Buy German blue rams from a shop whose fish are bright, eating, and not covered in spots, or from a seller who guarantees live arrival and packs them warm. The price range of about 5 to 100 dollars is wide because color lines and size vary, and a cheap dark fish is the expensive one if it dies in quarantine. Ask to see a feeding. Walk away from a tank of clamped rams no matter the sale. Acclimate slowly into a warm cycled quarantine. Intermediate care starts with refusing a sick animal, not with a medicine cabinet.

Read the ranges as a warm-water dwarf project, not a bargain tetra. About 100 to 500 dollars or more to set up, about 5 to 100 dollars per fish, about 200 to 500 dollars a year to run, and about 50 to 150 dollars in food, against a 3 to 4 year life in 20 gallons or more. People who save on the heater spend the fish money twice. Add a spare heater and test reagents to the yearly number. A peaceful ram still needs frequent water changes, and those changes are part of the 200 to 500 dollar upkeep, not an extra you invent later. The short lifespan makes skipped maintenance show up inside a single season.

Heat is the whole risk on this species. German blue rams are kept warmer than most community tetras, and a heater that fails off in a 20-gallon tank can drop them into a range where they clamp, darken, and break with ich by the next day. A heater that fails on is just as bad in that small volume, pushing a shallow sand bed hotter still while the fish sit in it. Put the thermometer at sand level and read it daily. Keep a second heater that can actually hold 20 gallons, not a giant unit that overshoots. If the filter stops, ammonia rises while the fish are already heat-stressed. A battery air pump keeps oxygen moving in an outage. It will not hold the warmth this ram needs, so insulation and a backup heat plan matter more than they do for a cool-water livebearer.

Buy heater quality before you buy a higher-grade ram. The fish can be inexpensive and still depend on a 20-gallon planted tank, a mature filter, and tankmates that took months to settle. A thermostat you cannot trust ends that project in a night, which is a large slice of a 3 to 4 year life. Choose equipment with a readable control and available parts. Replace a failing unit while the rams are still bright on the sand. The animals are intermediate because the margin is thin. Gear that wanders in temperature is the expensive choice, even when the sticker price looked thrifty.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress are visible on a glass catfish in a way they are not on an opaque fish: the body is clear, so a white grain, a red streak, or a clamped transparent fin shows if you look from the side. The usual cause is a broken school, a bright bare tank, or nitrite. Keep the group in 30 gallons or more, peaceful and together, and quarantine new cats as a school for a few weeks. They are intermediate because a lone Kryptopterus stops eating and fades. Do not reach for aquarium salt or a broad medicine as a first move. No dose is on this card, and a scaleless-looking transparent cat is a poor candidate for a guess. Ask a veterinarian if the school declines after the water tests clean.

Set up the 30-gallon tank as a quiet midwater lane before you buy glass catfish. They are peaceful schoolers, about 4 to 5 inches, with a 7 to 8 year lifespan, and a single specimen in a shop tank is already the wrong picture. Setup costs of about 100 to 500 dollars or more should buy length, a gentle filter, and cover. Fish can run about 5 to 100 dollars. Talk to keepers who have kept a group, not a solitary pet. They will mention dim light, company, and meaty foods that have to reach the middle of the tank. A catfish forum aimed at plecos will not describe this animal.

Leave the middle of the tank open and plant the back and sides. Glass catfish school in the water column and freeze when the layout keeps changing. A weekly rebuild makes an intermediate, peaceful species look fragile when it is mostly disoriented. Dim light and a dark background help you see the transparent bodies and help the fish settle. Add a plant if a corner is bare. Do not chase them with new ornaments. The habitat is a calm lane in 30 gallons or more, close to the slow shaded water they use in the wild.

Feed glass catfish in midwater at dusk, a small frozen or live item such as brine or daphnia, so the school has to move and you can count clear bodies against the light. Pellets that sink straight to the gravel miss the fish and feed whatever lives on the bottom. The hunt is the enrichment and the health check together. A cat that drifts with the group but never takes food has left the baseline of a 4 to 5 inch schooler. Test the water that evening. On a transparent fish, a missed feeding and a change in how the organs look through the body are the early signs you get.

Purchase glass catfish as a group from a shop that keeps them together in dim, clean water, or from a mail seller with a live-arrival guarantee. The card's span of about 5 to 100 dollars per fish is meaningless if you buy one. A solitary glass cat is a stressed animal, not a centerpiece. Refuse any group with spots, torn fins, or fish lying on the bottom. Quarantine the school as a school. Intermediate care is mostly this social fact plus water that stays at 0 ppm ammonia, for a peaceful fish that can live 7 to 8 years when the group stays intact.

Most gobies on this card are carnivores, and the food has to land where that species lives. A sand-sifting diamond goby needs fine foods on the sand bed in a tank large enough for a 6-inch fish, often the upper end of the 10 to 55 gallon range. A neon goby will take small meaty bites in the rocks. A firefish hovers and picks from the water. Hold the reef at 72 to 82°F, pH 8.1 to 8.4, and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, and feed a little mysis, brine, or a tiny marine pellet once or twice a day. Leftovers buried in sand push nitrate past 20 ppm. A vegetarian flake meant for a tang does not count as feeding a carnivore goby.

Match the rotation to the job the goby does. A sand-sifter still needs targeted frozen food after the bed is clean, or it starves in a spotless tank. A watchman goby sharing a burrow with a pistol shrimp may eat at the entrance and ignore food on the far glass. If a goby that used to dart for mysis now sits in the hole, check salinity and whether a tankmate has taken the burrow before you change brands. Three to 8 years, depending on species, is long enough for one food to become a nutritional rut. Refusal of a known favorite is the early health flag. The family label carnivore is the clue, and the species is the menu.

Feeding is diagnostic because gobies do not all eat in the same place. A yellow watchman should pop from the burrow, grab a morsel, and back in, often with a pistol shrimp maintaining the hole. A firefish should hover and pick. A clown goby stays in coral branches. If you only watch the open water, you will declare a healthy burrow goby a failed eater. Feed the spot the species actually uses, and feed enough times that a peaceful fish is not outcompeted by wrasses. Two gobies that want the same hole will not share a meal politely. Give each a burrow. Appetite at that burrow, at 72 to 82°F and the right salinity, tells you more than color under actinic light.

A goby that abandons its burrow, breathes fast, or shows white specks against the sand is having a bad day you should not sleep on. Marine ich and velvet move quickly at 72 to 82°F, and a fish already thin from losing the food fight has less margin. Learn the normal: sand-sifters work the bed, watchmen guard the hole, firefish hover. A dusty coat or a fish on its side on the sand is a different picture. Do not put copper in a reef. Invertebrates, including a pistol shrimp partner, die from copper. Move the goby to a fish-only hospital tank if you can, and involve a veterinarian. This page has no dose to copy.

Quarantine a new goby in marine water at 72 to 82°F and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, with sand or a PVC burrow so a watchman or a shrimp goby will eat. A firefish needs a lid on the quarantine tank too, because they jump. Several weeks of watching the species feed in its normal spot reveals ich and velvet before the fish meets a reef you cannot treat. Never dose copper in the display. If copper is used, it is a veterinarian's call in a fish-only tank, and the pistol shrimp stays behind. A sand-sifter starved in a bare cup during quarantine is not a successful observation. Give it something to sift and a pinch of food on that sand.

Thriving is a goby doing the job you bought it for, in a tank sized to the species. A neon goby picking pests in 10 gallons, a watchman at a burrow with its shrimp, or a diamond goby actually sifting in a bed deep enough, at 72 to 82°F and specific gravity 1.020 to 1.025, can live toward the 3 to 8 year span. Surviving is a firefish on the carpet because the lid was off, or a sand-sifter starving on a bare-bottom reef. If you will match the footprint inside the 10 to 55 gallon range, feed a carnivore diet, and keep a lid on the jumpers, the fish is a fair project. A single care level cannot cover every genus in Gobiidae. Read the species.

Costs follow the species and the box. A tiny clown goby in 10 gallons still needs salt, tests, and meaty frozen food. A 6-inch sand-sifter needs a deep sand bed and a tank toward 55 gallons, and the salt and electricity scale up. People budget the fish and then skip water changes, so nitrate climbs past 20 ppm and the goby stops sifting. Plan frozen mysis as a repeating purchase and a spare pump before a long weekend. A reef at 72 to 82°F does not wait while a part ships. The pistol shrimp, if you keep that partnership, is part of the livestock value a cheap failure will take with the goby.

Heater failure hits small goby tanks first. Ten gallons can leave 72 to 82°F in an afternoon if the heater sticks on, and evaporation at the same time drives specific gravity above 1.025 if nobody tops off with fresh water. A larger sand-sifter tank moves more slowly and is easier to ignore until the goby has left the burrow. A failed return pump is worse for a fish that lives in a hole: the burrow goes stale, oxygen drops, and the goby declines while midwater fish still look passable. Read the thermometer and the refractometer. Keep a spare heater matched to the gallons you run, and a small pump if the main one dies. Do not top off a hot tank with saltwater.

The lid, the heater, and the pump that keeps a burrow oxygenated are the purchases that protect a goby. Most of these species are reef-safe, so the corals and the pistol shrimp around them are the value a bargain heater destroys. Three to 8 years is long enough to wear out a pump. Buy the replacement while the first one still runs, and match it to a tank inside the 10 to 55 gallon span rather than to a generic reef kit. A firefish lid is not optional equipment. It is the difference between a hovering fish and a fish on the floor. Spend there, and on a thermometer you can read without moving the rock that holds the burrow.

Feed the gourami you actually have. A sparkling or honey gourami in 10 gallons takes a fine omnivore flake at the surface. A pearl or a blue gourami in 30 gallons can handle a small pellet and frozen food, and a male of the larger species will guard that food once he is in the mood. Hold the group at 74 to 82°F and pH 6.0 to 7.5. Offer what they finish, because leftover flake in a still corner, under a labyrinth fish that likes calm water, rots and lifts nitrate past 20 ppm. Do not feed a 2-inch honey the ration you would throw to a 6-inch three-spot. Four to 8 years of omnivore meals means portions matched to the species on the tag, at the surface where these fish expect to eat.

Rotate a flake or pellet with a frozen food so you can see appetite on a fish that also sneaks air at the surface. A honey gourami that ignores a favorite worm and hangs at the top corner is a different signal from a male pearl gourami that is simply full and building a bubble nest. Learn which you have. Refusal plus clamped feelers, fading color, or a sunken belly is the early illness picture across this group. One food for every gourami in the shop is how dwarf gouramis and giant gouramis get the same jar and the wrong amount. Note the species and the meal. The family is omnivore. The portion is not universal.

Gouramis feed at the surface and just under it, and the males of some species turn that into a territory. A honey or a pearl should come up calmly and take food. A blue or gold male may drive everyone else off the corner he has decided to nest in, which is the semi-aggressive end of this card and a reason those fish want 30 gallons rather than 10. Scatter the meal so a female still eats. If the whole tank refuses food and gasps under an oily film, you have a surface problem, not a picky fish. Labyrinth fish need air they can reach. Wipe that film, check 74 to 82°F, and then decide whether anyone is actually sick. Feeding behavior here is half hunger and half who owns the top of the tank.

Watch the feelers and the surface visit. A healthy gourami takes a gulp of air and goes back to the plants. A fish that hangs on the surface, feelers chewed short, body dark, is not just breathing. That picture, plus white specks or frayed fins, is the deviation to catch early. Dwarf gouramis add a separate problem: iridovirus is common in the trade, it has no home cure, and a dwarf that is already hollow should not be medicated hopefully and poured into a community. For ich or fin rot on the other species, clean water and quarantine do more than a random bottle. No dose is printed here. A veterinarian is the right call when a fish declines in water that already tests at 0 ppm ammonia.

Quarantine gouramis one species at a time, in a cycled tank at 74 to 82°F with access to humid air under a cover. A dwarf gourami should not share that tank with a pile of other new fish if you are trying to see whether it is a carrier of the iridovirus that haunts this species. Larger gouramis need enough surface that a male is not in permanent combat during the observation. A few weeks of eating and intact feelers is the bar. Do not dose the quarantine on arrival. If disease shows, keep it out of the display. Copper and random cures are a poor match for a labyrinth fish that is already breathing at the surface in distress.

Choose the gourami by the adult and the sex, and ask someone who has kept that species. A honey in 10 gallons is a shy peaceful fish. A pearl wants nearer 30 gallons and stays peaceful. A blue or opaline male can be a bully in the same 30 gallons, especially when he nests. Dwarf gouramis are the ones keepers will warn you about, because iridovirus cuts the 4 to 8 year lifespan down to a sad month. That conversation, species by species, is the decision. A single page that says gouramis are easy is how a semi-aggressive male ends up with a tank of shredded tankmates.

The satisfying gourami is the one whose size, sex, and tank match. A honey or a sparkling gourami in a planted 10-gallon tank at 74 to 82°F, feelers long, coming to the surface and then back to the leaves, is a good small fish. A pearl gourami schooling calmly in 30 gallons is a different and equally good picture. A male three-spot that owns the entire top of a too-small tank is the picture people regret. Four to 8 years is realistic when you pick the peaceful species on purpose and leave the surface clear. It is not realistic for a random male sold as a community fish.

Heater failure lands on gouramis as a surface crisis. At 74 to 82°F a 10-gallon honey gourami tank can overshoot or crash in hours, and the fish responds by hanging at the top, which looks like normal labyrinth breathing until you notice it never goes back down. A 30-gallon pearl or blue gourami tank moves slower, so a dead heater overnight in a cold room is easy to miss until the males are dark and the feelers are clamped. Read the thermometer at the surface, where these fish live. Keep a spare heater sized to the tank you have, 10 or 30 or larger, not a leftover from a different build. If the filter stops, ammonia and an oily film arrive together. An air stone helps, and it does not replace the filter or the warmth. Wipe the surface so they can still reach air while you fix the equipment.

Spend on a heater that holds 74 to 82°F and on a lid that leaves a humid air gap without letting a jumping gourami out. The fish themselves may be cheap. The tank they share, the plants, and a mature filter are not, and a dwarf gourami you quarantined carefully is wasted if the heater cooks the display. Larger males live toward 8 years, which is long enough to replace a pump. Buy the one you can get parts for. A gentle filter at the surface, not a waterfall that exhausts a honey gourami, is the other piece of gear that matches this family. Match it to the species' tank size, from 10 gallons up to 55, and service it before the flow dies under a nest.

Green terrors eat like the big cichlids they are, out in the open, and they remember who fed them. An 8 to 12 inch Andinoacara in 75 gallons or more should come forward for a pellet, a prawn, or an earthworm, then go back to digging. Scatter part of the meal if you keep a pair, or the larger fish takes all of it and the smaller one fades. They are semi-aggressive. Feeding time is when that shows up, especially once they have a spawning site. Do not keep tiny tetras in the same water and call the missing ones a mystery. Live and frozen foods are useful. They are also how a terror learns to bite fingers if you hand-feed carelessly. Use tongs, and watch whether both fish still eat. A terror that will not rise for a prawn has left a very obvious baseline.

Portions for an 8 to 12 inch omnivore are larger than for a ram and still finite. A cichlid pellet, earthworm, or market shrimp, eaten in a few minutes at a temperature appropriate for a South American cichlid, then removed, keeps a 75-gallon tank from becoming a nitrate factory. The card budgets about 50 to 150 dollars a year for food. That is enough if you are not dumping a handful because the fish begs. Begging is normal in a green terror. Obesity and filthy water are the usual result of believing it. Feed juveniles more often than a settled 12-inch adult. Twelve to 15 years of overfeeding is a long time to carry a swollen fish in a tank you cannot easily rehome.

A pellet day and a meaty day give you a way to read a green terror's appetite. This species will eat almost anything, so a refusal is meaningful. If a fish that usually inhales an earthworm turns away, darkens, and stays in a cave, stop shopping for new foods and test the water. Variety still matters over 12 to 15 years, because a single cheap pellet is a thin diet for a large omnivore, but the third new jar in a week is not medicine. Note what was eaten and by which fish of the pair. A semi-aggressive cichlid that suddenly shares, or suddenly will not, is telling you about dominance as well as health.

Ich, fin rot, bacterial infections, and stress from constant fighting are the health problems that show on green terrors. White spot on a big green body, ragged fins after a spat, and a fish pinned behind the filter are the usual views. Prevention is space, 75 gallons or more, a pair rather than a pile of adults, and water changes that match the waste of an 8 to 12 inch cichlid. Quarantine new fish for a few weeks. Catching a sick terror out of a decorated 75-gallon tank is a wet, destructive afternoon. Do not pre-dose salt or a broad medicine. Nothing on this card is a dose. If the fish declines in clean water, a veterinarian who will see a large cichlid is the next step.

The feeding approach is the exam. A healthy green terror should be bold, green and bright, fins out, taking food from tongs or from the surface without thrashing the whole tank. Your baseline is that confidence. A fish that hides, breathes fast, develops holes or white grains, or stops eating while its partner still comes forward has left it. Look at both animals. Semi-aggressive pairs can injure each other, and the injury looks like disease if you only glance. Catch the change while the fish still eats and still comes to the glass. A 12-inch cichlid off food under a pile of rock is a hard rescue, and this page will not hand you a treatment recipe.

Quarantine a green terror in a cycled tank big enough that an 8-inch fish can turn around, with a cave and a tight lid, before it meets your pair. They are semi-aggressive and they dig, so a small hospital bowl is both cruel and useless as an observation. Several weeks of normal appetite tells you whether you are importing ich into a 75-gallon system you do not want to tear apart. Do not medicate on arrival because large cichlids look tough. If spots appear, they stay in quarantine and a veterinarian sets the plan. Adding a new terror straight to a breeding pair is how the new fish gets killed and how any disease it carried gets distributed.

Before you buy a green terror, have 75 gallons or more cycled, filtered, and lidded, with a plan for the fish it will eat or beat. They are intermediate, semi-aggressive, and 12 to 15 years long. The card's setup range of about 100 to 500 dollars or more will not always build that tank, so treat it as a floor and talk to keepers who have housed an adult pair. They will mention digging, divorces between pairs, and tankmates that vanished. A beginner community thread will tell you the juvenile looks fine. The juvenile is not the fish you are agreeing to keep.

Give a green terror sand or fine gravel it can dig, a cave, and wood, and expect the planting to be rearranged. Rooted plants become debris. Tie hardy plants to rock if you want any green left. Do not rebuild the aquascape every weekend. A semi-aggressive pair treats every rebuild as a new border war. Move one dangerous sharp ornament out. Leave the spawning cave where the pair put it. The useful habitat in 75 gallons or more is open floor for digging and a sight-line break, not a delicate aquascape you will resent the fish for ruining.

Toss an earthworm or a prawn into the open and let a green terror hunt it, then hand a pellet with tongs if you want the interaction without the fingers. That hunt is the enrichment for a big omnivore, and it shows you whether the pair is still bold. Live foods from a clean source work. Feeder fish from a crowded tank are a parasite delivery system and a bad habit. If the terror will not move for a worm, believe the fish and test the water. On a cichlid of 8 to 12 inches, appetite is rarely subtle. The day it becomes subtle is the day you pay attention.

Buy green terrors from a shop that keeps large cichlids in clean, covered tanks and will show you a feeding, or from a seller with a live-arrival guarantee. About 5 to 100 dollars on the card buys a juvenile more often than a proven adult pair. Pay for a fish that eats and has intact fins, not for the biggest discount in a bruised tank. Quarantine it. A semi-aggressive species that arrives already sick becomes your problem in a tank that is hard to break down. Ask what else was in the shop tank. If the answer is a pile of dead tankmates, choose another fish.

Plan for a large cichlid's upkeep. Setup about 100 to 500 dollars or more, the fish about 5 to 100 dollars, yearly costs about 200 to 500 dollars, and food about 50 to 150 dollars, for an animal that needs 75 gallons and can live 12 to 15 years. Those yearly figures assume you actually change water and replace media on a filter sized for an 8 to 12 inch omnivore. People who buy the juvenile cheap later pay in emergency upgrades and in fish the terror has killed. Add a spare heater and a spare impeller to the year. Semi-aggressive and long-lived means the equipment decision is part of the livestock decision.

A green terror in 75 gallons has more thermal mass than a ram tank, which makes heater failure sneakier. The water cools overnight in a cold room, the fish darkens and stops coming up for food, and ich shows up a day later when you thought the heater had only just died. A stuck-on heater is slower to notice too, until the fish is gasping and the temperature is well above a normal tropical range. Read a thermometer you can see without moving the lid a big cichlid will hit. Keep a second heater that can hold 75 gallons, and aeration if the filter stops. An air pump in a power cut supplies oxygen to a large, oxygen-hungry fish. It does not remove the ammonia a 12-inch cichlid produces while the canister is off. Be ready to change water when the power returns.

Buy the canister, the lid, and the heater as if a 12 to 15 year semi-aggressive cichlid will test them, because it will. Green terrors move decor, splash, and produce waste that clogs cheap filters. The fish may sit at the low end of a 5 to 100 dollar range as a juvenile and still live in a 75-gallon system that costs far more to replace than the animal. A lid that lifts lets a startled terror onto the floor. A filter you cannot get parts for becomes a crisis in year six. Spend on serviceable equipment and replace a noisy pump while the pair is still eating. The tankmates that survive this species, and the mature filter that keeps up with it, are the value you are protecting.
